 Hard Time has been on my TBR for ages. One of my friends read it and raved about it a couple years, so I promptly bought it... and then never got around to reading it. Something that seems pretty common in my world, honestly. It wasn't until I was chatting with a group of author friends at Apollycon and it came up again that I decided it was high time I finally read it. Part of me hates that it took this long to get around to it, but the other part is just grateful I finally made time to read it. Because holy crap. What a book. 
 Despite there being several books with a similar premise on my eReader and shelves right now, this is the first time I've read a book with an inmate for a hero. I wasn't sure I'd be able to get into it, even though it really is one of the ultimate forbidden romances, I suppose. That might be why I waited so long to read i, if I'm being totally honest. Any preconceived notions I had about what an "inmate romance" might be like were totally off-base. Starting, of course, with the hero himself. Because my gods, Eric. Eric was amazing. He's easily one of my new favorite book boyfriends of 2017. His crime didn't make him a bad man, neither did the time he spent behind bars. Sure, he was a bit hard... but he was also sweet, sensitive and really easy to fall for. Annie was a fantastic heroine, too. First and foremost, I applauded her work as librarian with the inmates. Not everyone would be brave enough to be willing to put themselves through what she did to try to help others. I appreciated how she worked to make a difference in these men's lives. She was timid and reserved, but slowly came out of her shell thanks to Eric. 
 I loved so much how these two characters came together. The initial chemistry was one thing, but the real fun began when they started exchanging letters. (Which, naturally, was forbidden.) The letters were HOT, but it wasn't all about sex. Yes, there was SERIOUS sexual tension between these two, but there was more than that building as well. There was a sexual reawakening of sorts, but it was more than that. These two characters truly brought out the best in each other, thoughts and feelings that had been locked away for years... for both of them. Eric might've been the one behind bars, but Annie was locked up in her own way, too. I'm not accustomed to seeing this much growth in characters outside the YA and NA books I read. It was such a pleasant surprise here. 
 It was one thing to open up and write letters to an inmate, but things became real and incredibly complicated once Annie learned Eric was being released. Could what started under unconventional circumstances translate into the real world? Did she want it to? Would he? So many unanswered questions. I was so wrapped up in the gorgeous writing and these characters I'd fallen hard as hell for that I felt like I was the one making the tough decision here. Of course, I'm not going to tell you anything more about the plot. It's one you just need to experience for yourself. 
 Hard Time was a great book. It was borderline addictive and I couldn't get enough. Now that I've discovered my love for Cara McKenna's writing, I'm going to have no choice but to devour her backlist. 
 FAVORITE QUOTES 
 His gaze dropped from my eyes to my mouth, the weight of it as real as a kiss.

 I want to escape inside you. I want to feel your hands on me, and your eyes, and feel like there's nobody else for a hundred miles.

"Maybe we're like the cherry blossom, Rune. Like shooting stars. Maybe we loved too much too young and burned so bright that we had to fade out." 
 Welp. My opinions are all over the place. I've been putting off writing about A Thousand Boy Kisses since June. This made it into the opening rounds of the GR choice awards months ago, so at the time, it seemed a good time to attempt a review that will get buried. I'm super bad about writing reviews anymore. 
 A personal, relevant factoid: I've always been the kind of person who loves sad things. Almost nothing makes me happier than crying over fictional worlds that I could never be part of, or listening to songs I wish I had written, among other imaginary escapades. It sounds depressing but I'm fine like that. Once in a while, flying through a book that sweeps me off my feet with poignant writing and characters who go through so much that it moves me to tears is the perfect escape from reality. 
 That's why I bought and read ATBK in a day and a half. Sure, it sounded like it could have been a corny, gushy story judging from the title alone, but I took my chances. 
 Man did it deliver! Every other chapter made me a blubbering, runny-nosed mess. This book tore me open. So much so, that I'm not sure if I could relive these character's tragedies all over again. It was too painful. Coming from someone who loves sad things, that is a hell of a strong statement, and I still stand by that even though I read the book eight months ago. 
 Now here's where the confusing part comes in. 
 ATBK did try really hard to be the latest and greatest Cancer Love Story(c), a la The Fault in Our Stars or A Walk To Remember. Some elements of it felt a little forced and melodramatic in order to give your tear ducts a workout. The main lovers-Poppy and Rune-repeat the same sweet nothings to each other during serious moments, such as "For infinity" or "Forever and always." The subject matter of the book gives the perfect backdrop for tons of serious moments where they would make these statements over and over, and it got...tiring. 
 Since I'm a little older than the target audience, Poppy and Rune's relationship for half the book seemed almost obsessive to me. Always wanting to be alone together, even when they're hanging out with mutual friends. Making out no matter who is around. Not going a single day without talking to and seeing each other. I don't know if it's my age or how I "juzt dont understand tru luv!!!" or both, but their infatuation kind of annoyed me. 
 If there's something good I can say about the leads is that they weren't as pretentious as Hazel and Augustus in The Fault in Our Stars. Poppy was a sweet character with a touch of Manic Pixie Dream Girl, while Rune was flawed yet interesting. I enjoyed reading about their little adventures and travels. I also thought their relationship made more sense than Hazel and Augustus'. Poppy and Rune were neighbors for a decade, grew up together, and were there for each other at their worst. If there's a more perfect way for fictional leads to fall in love, I haven't found it yet. 
 Like I mentioned in the beginning, the writing was poignant and pretty and not too "purple." I really enjoyed the flow. Three or four minor spelling errors were made, but I've seen worse. 
 And now my buddy my pal, let's talk about TEH ENDING. *cracks knuckles* I can buy the whole "collecting 1,000 paper hearts that equal 1,000 kisses" shebang. What went down at the end was just too Hallmark channel-esque. And WHY OH WHY was it never explained how Rune died in the epilogue? Did he get in an accident? Did he succumb to heartbreak or did he get cancer too? I just really hope it's not suicide, cause I personally feel as though that would be a bad message.  Ultimately, it is a happy-though very bittersweet-ending. I'm still not sure what I think about it overall. I just can't decide if everything was tied up too neatly or if I appreciated the author's attempts to put a balm over her reader's hearts. Probably the latter. 
 This whole book left me indecisive. That doesn't mean I hated it or even disliked it, don't get me wrong. My verdict is that I would read more books by Ms. Cole if they aren't as emotionally draining as ATBK.

When I picked up Overprotected I expected to read a nice, light, fluffy read. I had high hopes to start but not even halfway through it, I found myself skimming some parts... And kinda repetitive. 
 Both Ashlyn and Colin were pretty okay but not well-developed. I hate to say this but they lacked substance. And although I sympathized with her, she still annoyed me. And there was practically no character development of Colin... There's absolutely no chemistry between them! Na-da! i couldn't quite get emotionally invested in Colin and Ashlyn. 
 Overall, Overprotected was an okay read about overprotective and paranoid dad, I didn't enjoy the book as much I'd hoped I would. By no means, did I hate the book, but I felt like it left quite a bit to be desired. This is my first book by the author. and though I don't really like this one, I'm not quitting on her yet!

I have to say that I was a bit hesitant going into this installment because Ice Like Fire dragged so much in the first half of the book. I didn't want this to face the same fate. I didn't want one my favorite series to have a "meh" ending. However, I found this to be a really satisfying conclusion. 
 I have really enjoyed how with each installment, Raasch has added another POV. I was super excited to see that in this one we would be hearing from Ceridwen, who quickly became one of my favorite characters. She is so feisty and really compliments Meira's personality well. I love the friendship that developed between these two immensely strong and powerful women. However, I did find it a little strange that Meira was told from a first person POV while Ceridwen and Mather were told from third person POVs. I understand the reasoning because Meira is our main girl and the other two characters serve to give insight into conflicts in other areas of the kingdom, but I still found it to be awkward at times. It made it difficult to connect to the story or characters in some instances and made me like I was observing some scenes rather than experiencing them with the characters. 
 Like many YA series, this one does feature a love triangle. However, I never felt like it was overemphasized or overshadowed the true conflicts in the story. I also never really felt invested in one side or the other. I didn't feel like either relationship was really well developed or highlighted in the first two books. In this installment, it definitely plays a larger role. I can say that with certainty because I barely remember any development of it at all in books one and two; like, I don't understand why Meira likes either of the boys or vice versa. However in this book, I distinctly remember several scenes between Meira and one of the boys. The relationship become much more memorable in this installment. I went from not caring who she chose to being really invested and emotional about the relationship that was featured in this book. 
 In the end, I am extremely satisfied with the conclusion of this trilogy. There is a substantial epilogue that chronicles the events after climax that quelled my investments in these characters. That is, I feel like I have a good sense of everyone's life direction and well-being. I love when series end this way. I cannot to reread and enjoy this trilogy again in the future. 
 I would definitely recommend this to lovers of high fantasy and to those who are just getting their feet wet. It has a beautifully rich world but isn't too complex to be unapproachable for new-to-fantasy readers. 
 I am anxiously looking forward to reading Raasch's future novels :)

I didn't finish this trilogy feeling awe struck or out of breath, but I did feel very satisfied and honestly content. I suppose that is exactly the perfect feeling to have about a series that always prided itself on being extremely realistic -and rightfully so- Because life hardly ever leaves you awe struck, That's why we read. So the best you could hope for is to feel content at the end. 
 And I say that with the wisdom/ hallucination that comes after spending the whole night reading, right until 9 in the morning. 
 Now speaking about the ending in a more practical sense, you should know that no loose ends remained and each and every character got their satisfactory end. I don't think anyone was slighted in the slightest, not even the minor characters. So truly this was a perfect end. 
 However it wasn't the perfect book, hence the-one-star-lower-than-the-last-two-books rating. There wasn't anything wrong with the book, it was interesting enough and everything was alright, it just somehow impressed me less than the last ones, and I felt like I should somehow acknowledge that in the rating. 
 Speaking about the trilogy as a whole, I am extremely happy I read it. I have a feeling some scenes from it are going to be truly long lived in my memory, both in the horror and in the joy department, and to be honest sometimes I think that is all I want from a book.

There are a lot of smart, funny quips that you would expect from Tina Fey. I loved the bits about "car creepery", the anecdote about Amy Poehler, experiences with working in comedy, and other observations about gender and contemporary issues. Told in her trademark style, these insights and stories show what there is to love about Tina Fey, and they're the highlight of the book. 
 Other aspects of the book are less remarkable. Many notable experiences or traits of Fey's are either barely touched on or talked about at length without offering much new or interesting information. Fey almost seems reluctant to discuss certain topics, only including them because it's expected. I wish she'd either committed to exploring these aspects and found a new angle for them or left them out entirely. The book would be great as a collection of essays about feminism and working in entertainment, but it doesn't really work as the tell-all memoir that many expected. 
 Also, it's definitely a book to listen to. The tone is occasionally awkward to read, but it works well read in Tina's voice.

Seventeen year old Mia has everything going for her- a loving family, great boyfriend, loyal best friend, and a good chance at getting into Julliard. Then one morning after a freak snow storm, the car her family is traveling in is hit by a four-ton pickup truck. The first thing Mia realizes as she steps out of the car onto the embankment is that she can still hear the music playing on the car stereo. For a moment, this leads her to believe that everything is OK. Then she sees her parents and knows instantly that both are dead. She looks frantically for her brother and thinks she has found him until she looks more closely and realizes that she is staring down at her own unconscious body. Mia watches as the paramedics come and take her to the hospital. She watches as the doctors work on her, trying to keep her alive. She watches as her grandparents and friends sit by her bedside. And while she watches she remembers her life up until the accident. Eventually, she realizes that it is up to her to decide whether she wants to fight for her life. She thinks about whether or not she is strong enough to deal with the pain of having lost her family. Does she want to fight to live in a world without her family or would she rather simply let go and pass on with them? If I Stay is a beautifully written novel with well developed characters that will make readers put themselves in Mia's shoes and consider what it would be like to go living when the people you love the most are gone.

Rating: 2/5 
 I don't know why I had to complete the series. I mean, I didn't like the pacing of the story: breakneck with no character development or at least no meaningful and natural character development. There were too many characters to care about any one of them. Josh annoyed the heck out of me. Sophia was likable but not enough to really care and that's our two main characters and then Nicholas and Penny ('m not going to type her whole name as as I'm not going to type the whole names of the gods save for the simple ones) who seems or should be forefront characters (as Penny is married to Nicholas and Nicholas' name is in the series' title) took a back seat to the entire thing. Then things just happen for reason being solely: just cuz. So why did I pick it up? I enjoyed the Shadowrealm concept and I enjoyed the mythology in the book. I said it before in other reviews: I'm a big mythology fan so as this one was so littered and inspired by world mythology I had to pick it up and unfortunately I also don't like leaving things unfinished. 
 I'm going to make this review short. Yes, I have read the other books in the series. Yes, this one is the ending. The only good things about this book were the ideas behind the concept and plot and the action. That's about it. The characters were close to being flat. Emotions and scenes were imposed onto to them in such a way that it didn't seem believable or remained poignant, thus rendering the characters as such too. I'm not saying there weren't any scenes that attempted to bring the characters to life cause there were (like Scathy going to Danu Talis to see if she was like her dad), but everything moved at such a fast pace that it really didn't mattered. Add the fact that we are following over ten characters and thus their stories become shortened and doesn't matter in the big picture. Emotions were painted onto characters because they should feel them the scene rather than the scene evoking the feel. 
 The magic became unbelievable. Creatures and immortals flung about magic like it was nothing, having no consequences. People claim to have a low aura and so they must save their aura's to stay alive and yet they continuously do magic... constantly... even Nicky and Penny used magic all the time to the end... even though you know they supposedly were low on magic... no one ever ran out of magic. Well no one human... the Elders were like storm troopers.... they killed each other, killed a lot and died and no one cared about them really. At least I didn't. Well, to be fair I didn't really care about any of the characters but it's sad to think that I cared even less about the Elders. So there were no consistent rules behind the magic. Magic fed off auras... but even then when someone's aura should have ran out they didn't. I also find it very hard to believe that an immortal human could defeat a god/goddess. But it happens even when there are other moments and scenes that reject the idea. Say the huge crab scene... they needed to wake an Ancient Elder (or was she just an Elder too many sub genre of "gods") cause everyone else is too weak... see there was a hierarchical scale of greatness and power... and yet those that are supposedly deemed the weakest: immortals, the rules don't apply to them. Yeah I don't think so. 
 Then comes the time paradox. So are we reading a cycle or something else? I mean clues were dropped in previous books and I thought then that it couldn't be... but it was... so the time jumping made the ending very anti-climatic in my opinion. We already knew what was going to happen if you know what I mean and it just goes in a circle... only kinda... cause some things weren't well explained and some characters had no closure or any hint of what happened to them... 
 Overall, the story is fast paced so nothing lulls. The idea and concept behind the story was strong but the execution was cluttered and clunky. Did I enjoy the story? Not really. Did I hate the series/book? I could care less. So not really... 
 Verdict: I would ultimately say pass. There are other series, fantastical in nature, to choose from.

I really liked the book. Kitty disgusted me more in the book, but that's to be expected. She is a spoiled rich kid who has never lived outside of her parents' home. The film takes many liberties and embellishments with many of the characters but they are not out of place. The screenplay follows pretty closely to the book with small differences. Yet in saying that, I don't know the relationship between the nuns and Kitty would've worked out as well on screen. They have very little dialogue but many interactions. Mr. Walter Fane was pretty much nonexistent, but that makes sense since we are mostly in Kitty's head and we have to take her word for every interaction that happens. 
 Kitty is spoiled and narrow-minded when the novel starts. She changes a tiny bit before the end. Don't go into this book with the idea that she will have a major transformation. She has small subtle changes and above, as she states, she's only human. It takes time for us to look back on our upbringing and experiences and reflect on their importance in the grand scheme of life. She begins to do a bit of that towards the end of the novel. For me, that definitely showed me that she had matured a tiny bit. As people, we change a tiny bit daily. What opinion you have one day, you many not have again the next day or the next week. With information and experience, opinions are changed and shaped. Kitty starts to see that indirectly. 
 W. Somerset Maugham's writing is approachable and engaging. I cannot wait to pick another one of his novels. The sense of setting in this novel is very strong and beautiful. Another aspect that they portrayed well in the film. Her characters were strong and enjoyable. 
 All in all, if you enjoyed the film, I think you should read the book. If you enjoyed the book, I think you should see the movie. They are similar and dissimilar all at once. W. Somerset Maugham's writing is approachable and engaging. I cannot wait to pick another one of his novels.

The Vegetarian by Han Kang is a quick read, whose simple prose is a social commentary of mental illness, gender roles and veganism in South Korea. The novel, divided into 3 "novellettes", is told by three family members' perspectives of a South Korean woman, Yeong-hye and her choice to become a vegan. 
 Section (1) is told by Yeong-hye's husband, who lacks empathy and is narcissistic in his own right. Section (2) is told by her brother-in-law, who is a struggling artist suffering from his own sexual demons. 
 Section (3) is told by Yeon-hye's sister, who tries to keep it all together while Yeong-hye is in the mental institution and while her own marriage falls apart. 
 I really enjoyed this novel. However, I wish I knew what Yeong-hye's voice was throughout the novel. I chose this novel to read for two reasons: (1) it was on the 2016 Man Booker's short list (which was just recently chosen as the winner) and (2) from the author's commentary printed in the New York Times: Han Kang explained she was "thinking about the spectrum of human behavior from sublimity to horror, and wondered if it was really possible for humans to live a perfectly innocent life in this violent world, and what would happen if someone achieved that?"

No wonder Zafron's book was a bestseller in Spain, and the translation has been equally a hit for English readers. A bibliophile's dream, an enigma involving a mysterious author. It is an atmospheric story set in post war Barcelona. The twists of plot are page turners and characters of such dimension they come alive. While the story swirls around one central character, it is really multiple tales of individual struggles in love, hatred, survival and power.

3.5 to be more precise. At first glance, you'd think this was a typical fairytale with the overused plotline between best friends who are polar opposites turning against each other. In a school of magic. Umm, magic? towering castles and whatnots? this book will sure have a hard time with me. But fear not, this one proves to be more than what meets the eye. 
 Let's focus first on the stuff that I don't like. The cover. I know a lot of people would disagree with me but you can't blame me for cringing at it. But as cliche goes, don't judge a book by its cover so all's settled. Second,  The part with the Schoolmaster finding for his true Evil love, just NADA. NA-UHH. His whole character confuses me af. Professor Sader as well, I mean I pretty much like him all throughout the book but his character development went into a turmoil for me esp. in the last part.  Third, it seems that this book failed to answer where the children are from and the actual scope of other villages. Well, it's a trilogy for a reason so I hope I'll get my answers on the sequels. Lastly, the unexpected change in POV's, I always lose track because in every chapter, POV's change frequently, although some seem to glue coherently but its confusing sometimes. I wish it was more like on the ratio of one chapter:one POV. 
 Moving on to the stuff I like! This one sure is beautifully written. No argument in that. Second, I love how this book took a darker path. When I say it's dark, that means YOU BETTER READ THIS RN. I can't believe that behind this puny cover ( no offense but it sucks.) lies a breadcrumb trail of surprises. The entire journey with the characters facing their inhibitions and finding their true selves is portrayed by the author in a way where a lot of people can relate to (or so I think). I like Agatha and Sophie's paradoxical friendship and overall, it was a nice read for me.

I have no words that will do this book justice. This book is perfect in every way, from the imperfect and fractured characters, the 1986 setting, the mixtapes, walkmans, and lack of mobiles, to the raw emotional journey it took us through Eleanor and Park; two teenagers who can't seem to find a place that they belong to, an identity they could proudly call their own, a "someone" they could turn to for help, for love, for friendship.. until they met each other. This book is so powerful. I read it in a couple of hours and I couldn't put it down. The two POVs, switching between Eleanor and Park, gave the readers more insight on what each side is feeling, thinking, and wishing. Something we don't usually witness. These characters were layered, had flaws, faults, and a history that would bring the readers emotional pain, allow them to connect with the characters, and root for them to get together, stay together, and be whoever they wanted and needed to be. 
 Rainbow Rowell's gift in writing should not be overlooked. She was able to create such an eloquent novel from a simple setting, Eleanor and Park sitting in the bus on the same chair. That is how they met, that is when we see them together for over 100 pages.. they barely talk, they barely communicate, heck, Eleanor calls him "the stupid asian kid" while Park is just trying to pretend she doesn't exist. Eleanor isn't the stick thin girl, no she is not obese, but she still has baby fat and people make fun of her, for that and her outrageous sense of style and bright red hair. They call her "Big Red". However Eleanor ignores them, for the most part, and tries to not let them get to her. However after she and Park started talking, communicating, and getting to know each other, the bullying took a step back. Yes bullying was still a part of the novel, but me as a reader lived for the moments that Eleanor & Park met because I believed they were the most gratingly honest and through them you just couldn't help but fall in love with them. 
 The story is more than a love story, it also includes an abusive relationship, Eleanor's mother and her step father; How I loathed him. I also did not have any happy thoughts towards Eleanor's mother. She has 4 small children, excluding Eleanor, and she still stays in that abusive relationship, stays with the man that kicked Eleanor out of the house for a full year. There is honestly so much family issues and all of them are so realistic which is why they all hit me hard, because many people suffer from being tied to such abusive relationships, and children being the helpless victims to that. I have to say though, I loved Park's family, he is half korean, and his dad loves his mom, so glaringly obvious that it really gives the readers a clear contrast between both families. I would have to say that every single young adult reader must pick this book. Whether they enjoy contemporary or not, this book is not one to miss. I am definitely going to be getting and cherishing a copy when it is out. Rowell, you officially made me a die hard fan.

 Unusually, this is a book without a villain- there are antagonists, but as the title intimates, they are not defeated but rather brought into alignment with the protagonists via compromise. There are no irredeemable or even wicked characters, but rather people with differing flaws and agendas struggling to get their way and believing themselves in the right. Goewin, the main character, even identifies with and at times parallels the villain of the first book. 
 The setting is also worth noting- ancient Ethiopia, where the British Goewin flees from her war-torn country, in a neat reversal. 
 Many tropes from the first book repeat- fraught sibling relationships, the problem of lesser royalty, accepting you won't rule, physical abuse and punishment, defiance, the rulers mishandling relationships but then redeeming themselves, a hunt on which loyalties are tested and forged. The plot and setting, however, are quite different. 
 You have to love a YA book where the main motif is the Song of Songs, and the female protagonist is described as "terrible as an army with banners."

EDIT: I just re-read this book and decided to give it 5 stars. I just wanted to thank Rainbow Rowell for writing Eleanor's story. It helped me find peace at a difficult time and I think it will for many others. Thank you for describing the vulnerability and helplessness survivors of family and domestic violence feel. You help me remember how much stories can save and comfort us. You reminded me that I'm not alone and for that, I'm grateful. 
 "It was the nicest thing she could imagine. It made her want to have his babies and give him both of her kidneys." 
 Okay, I'll be honest, after reading Fangirl I was left sorta disappointed and didn't know what to expect from this book. Maybe it was just another overly hyped book? But I was so wrong and I devoured this book in a matter of a few days. Eleanor & Park is a nerdy, cute yet dark coming-of-age story. A bit like a 1980s version of Romeo and Juliet. Reading this book reminded me of what it's like to be full of teenage angst and hopelessly in love. If you want your emotions to be slayed read this book. 
 This book is set in 1986, which is different for a YA contemporary novel published in 2013. Eleanor is a plump freckled redhead with an eccentric fashion style. She likes to wear plaid shirts, ties and jeans with holes in them. As soon as she gets on the school bus, she becomes an easy target for bullying. But a boy named Park moves over so she can sit down with him on the bus. Park is half-Korean, half-Irish and loves listening to music on his walkman. Oh, and he likes reading comic books like X-Men. 
 My heart swells up when I think about how they fell in love reading comic books on the bus. When they first held hands, I kept texting my fiance over and over again. I just couldn't help but get the gushy feels when I read that. I was rooting for them! 
 Rainbow Rowell is a great writer who knows how to create well-developed characters. Eleanor was so genuine and had the girl-next-door vibe going for her. She was the type of person you probably grew up with in middle school. She doesn't have the perfect family and grows up poor. The author does a good job of depicting the confusion and angst that comes with living in a dysfunctional environment. 
 You understand what you're going through is unfair and dangerous, but you feel like there's nothing you can do to help your situation. You see Eleanor going through an internal battle with herself throughout the book because she wants to call the police, but she's scared about her stepdad lashing out on her mom and siblings. This describes how I (and probably lots of other people) sometimes felt growing up with in my family. 
 Park grows up in a much different environment than Eleanor. His parents are well-off and can afford to feed him all 4 food groups. But he doesn't let his privileged upbringing take away from his ability to empathize with Eleanor. I'm a hopeless romantic and I live for stories like this. Park just loves Eleanor so much and does whatever he can to protect her. I think that's beautiful. I think every awkward and insecure teenage girl needs a friend like Park in their lives. 
 Spoiler Warning 
 What was that ending though? This novel broke my heart and left me wanting a sequel like right now. Even though Rainbow Rowell has assured us she's not quite done with these characters yet, I can't help but wonder what happens to them.. When the story begins, you know Eleanor and Park are going to get separated but you just don't know when . When Eleanor moves away to be with her uncle, I almost felt angry at her for not responding to Park. They could have been in a long-distance relationship! But I think it was the only way Eleanor knew how to deal with her sadness. 
 I hope the last 3 words she sends him are, "I love you" or "nothing ever ends". But whatever they are, I hope they're positive and help Park find his way back to Eleanor. The ending made me upset, but I think that's what the author wanted. The cliff hanger helps emphasize the uncertainty of falling in love at a young age. As you grow, time passes and life changes you. And I think even though we want to believe Eleanor and Park will be together forever, we'll never know just like they'll never know. 
 Spoiler End 
 I would definitely recommend reading this book. It was cute, without being overly fluffy. Just give it a chance and trust the hype!

 Game of Thrones meets Graceling in this striking fantasy tale of dark magic, dangerous politics, and discovering your true self. Sara Raasch's debut fantasy is a lightning-fast story of loyalty, love, and controlling one's destiny. 
 It would be pretty nice if what was promised in the blurb all came true. 
 Meira & Co are outcasts, the remaining eight citizens of Winter who have not been taken into captive as slaves, after losing a war with the Spring kingdom. Throughout the novel they spend their time trying to recapture the Winter kingdom back, and to find the two halves of a locket. The locket, when fixed, holds magic that would restore Winter into its former glory. 
 At the beginning, Meira is portrayed as a whiny, utterly incompetent brat that can't win a sword fight despite training for years. Her companions (all fighters) comes back bleeding and bruised. When Sir, the leader, refuses to let her go on a highly dangerous journey, she makes it her point to antagonise everyone. 
 Then Meira suddenly turns out to be a badass chakram throwing, dagger wielding fighter that can run on rooftops. 
 She complains constantly. It is a reoccurring theme in the novel; there is always something to moan about. She is reckless and immature at the beginning, and she continues to do so. The author writes it off as something admirable. Oh see, her recklessness allow her to recover a lost item! It allows her to discover secret plans so conveniently hid over there! Meira's recklessness continuously solve problems and progresses the plot, it is nothing more than deus ex machina. 
 The redeeming part of the novel is Meira's personal growth throughout her journey. When she is finally entrusted to a vital role she grows to accept it. "If only because, every morning, I find a way to be me." Meira is willing to participate in duties that she dislikes, yet regain some part of herself. She spends as much time learning etiquette as well as on the training field throwing her chakram. 
 "I've been so selfish, haven't I? Selfish and narrow-minded and wrong, because I wanted to matter to Winter, but in my own way." Meira knows what is expected of her, and proves that she truly wants to fulfil her part, even until the very end. For that, I admire her. 
 I do not believe that there is a love triangle in Snow Like Ashes, as she harbours a crush on each respective 
 very good looking 
 boy, but Meira does not proclaim, in any instance, of undying love. Neither does she spend all her waking hours thinking about the two; here Meira is like any other teenage girl. 
 One thing that I could not swallow is the setting. In Primoria there is a source of magic deep underground, and the four kingdoms built on the area above are named after the four seasons respectively, so we have the countries Spring, Summer, Fall and Winter. And yes, the climate and weather of each kingdom is parallel to the season it is named after. 
 Winter's capital city is Jannuari, an example of many incidents of lazy world building and bad spelling, and citizens of Winter are Winterians, Autumn's Autumnians, etc. What happens when you build countries in between the four? Then there are four countries outside of the magic area like Ventral or Yakim because yes, we need to now put in some vaguely fantasy sounding names. I believe that the world building is actually the weakest part of the novel. 
 The novel's magic system is even more headdesk worthy. Dark magic is a laughable concept, and very fitting in the black and white, good and evil theme of the novel. Magic is turned dark when it is used for "evil purposes", a very ambiguous term. The protagonist is good and all that apposes are evil. The man behind the destruction and cruelty of Winter and more is evil because he wants power. He has no real purpose or backstory; he is nothing more than a sorry caricature. 
 Instead of explaining the lore of magic, all Meira says in her many info dumps that is that nobody knows how magic came to be in their world. The original source of magic (deep underground) is still there, but the path to it is still blocked, supposedly in Winter. Each monarch of their respective kingdom wants to find it, but why don't they use their own magical object to locate the source? If they could use their magical objects to control armies like chess piece, it sure can be used to be a goddamn compass. 
 Wait, did I just find a solution to all of the 425 pages worth of problems?

So...that happened. 
 The short version is this: Suma has a way with words and I would most likely read her future works, but this story just didn't do it for me. 
 The long version is this: the intellectual in me is going "huh?" but the reader in me is going "what the fuck ever..." 
 The premise is interesting, some kind of psychological, are-there-such-things-as-ghosts thriller. Personally, I like answers and neatness, and most books in that category do not provide these things, but I'm not taking off points for that. I can sum up most of my problems in a few distinct categories. 
 First was the pace of the book. In the beginning there's the requisite set up of the perfect older sister, Ruby, and the utterly ordinary younger sister, Chloe. Yet Ruby loves Chloe with a force that is palpable, and would be worrisome in its obsessiveness if not for the purity of it. Chloe is sort of treated as gold by the other kids, not because they like her one way or the other, but because she's Ruby's sister. Chloe in turn idolizes her sister, but no more so than anyone else in town does. She's the "girls want to be her, guys want to be with her" type. Cool. Then one night with all the local kids hanging out at the reservoir, Chloe discovers the body of her classmate in the water. We later learn the girl, London, OD'd. Chloe leaves town shortly thereafter to go live out of state with her father (not Ruby's father), we presume to escape the shock and trauma of what happened that night. Fast forward two years later, when Ruby returns demanding Chloe go back with her. Though her father says no, Chloe catches a bus back to town and home to Ruby. 
 We're introduced to the surreal plot fairly early on, when at yet another local kids gathering, London is among them. Chloe of course is freaked out by that (more on that later) but no one else in town seems to remember that London died two years ago. And even more shocking than that, Ruby appears to cater to and protect London, almost as a surrogate baby sister in Chloe's absence. 
 But then, nothing really happens. For a looooooooooooong time. Sure, some more weird things happen, but mainly weird in that it's out of character for Ruby. And said events are rather minor and don't seem connected to anything. So the plot doesn't move forward. At all. It's just chapters upon chapters of "hmmm, that's odd." Which does not make for good reading. 
 Second: Chloe's response. Now, if I were to return home after two years to find a girl whose body I found alive and well and nobody seemed to notice, I'd probably ask the person I was closest to in the world wtf was going on. But Chloe doesn't do that. She tries, here and there, but Ruby usually completely changes the topic, like "hey what do you want for dinner." And Chloe just gives up. If I said "hey, didn't that girl die" and my sister responded with "hey, you should cut bangs in your hair" I'd probably respond with "no, seriously what's up with the dead girl." Chloe NEVER pushed the issue, and even for a story about dead girls and ghosts, I found that hard to swallow. No matter what happened, every time Ruby distracted her with a nonsequitur, she just dropped it like there weren't fucking ghosts running the streets. What in the ever loving fuck? 
 Three: character development. So Ruby is totally the It girl in town, even though there's something off about her. Not in a crazy way, per se, but she clearly knows a lot more about London than she's telling, for one, and after a while you start to think she had something to do with London coming back to life. But it's important to know that Ruby is idolized by everyone in town. Until about 3/4 of the way in. Chloe is hanging out with some guys, Ruby's not there, and they start lighting into Ruby, basically calling her a slut. But these are the same kids that have up to now practically kissed the ground she walks on. Chloe of course gets angry, and then London taunts her further, saying that everyone in town hates Ruby. What? No they don't! Since when? And why do they act like they worship her if cruelty they hate her? 
 Now I thought we were getting somewhere interesting, but this is never fucking mentioned again. What??? Why? Huh!??!?! 
 On reflection, it could have been that the kids were scared of her. But (1) give that the story is told from Chloe's point of view, who actually does idolize Ruby, this is more conjecture on my part than anything, since (2) there's nothing else provided in the story to warrant that leap. 
 And then there was Owen. I can't begin to explain the head-desking that his part incited. At one point, Owen accuses Chloe of being just like Ruby. We are led to believe this is an insult, as Owen seems to be one of the few people in town immune to Ruby's charm. But the comment comes out of fucking nowhere. Once again, the kids are just all hanging out, and she probably gives him the longing glance that 16-year-old girls with crushes are wont to do, and he walks up to her and is all F you, you're just like Ruby. This scene is impossibly made even more confusing that NOTHING has happened to give rise to this claim. Not a goddammed thing. Out of the clear blue... How she's like Ruby or what she has done to give Owen that impression, God only knows. Again, as crazy as teenagers are, this seemed patently ridiculous. Now, I guess I could theorize that he decided he didn't like her and thought being mean to her would get rid of her (aren't boys awesome?), but once again, that's just me making shit up. 
 Ultimately, I probably could have dealt with holes in the conclusion - not really knowing what happened to London, or what Ruby's role was, whether the whole thing was a dream or something. But the holes in the underlying story and the plot was just too much.

 Another winner from Le Guin. Everything about her writing works wonders for me (although I know this won't be true for everyone). The amount that she manages to pack into this novella without it feeling too dense is amazing. 
 One of my favorite parts is a small detail: the fact that most the Athshean words have double or triple meanings, some even close to becoming contradictory. The fact that their word for 'god' also means 'translator' is so fascinating and adds a great deal to the character of Selver without Le Guin having to spend time revealing those layers outright. 
 Another of my favorite aspects of the story was that few of the characters are entirely likable. Even idealists like Lyubov have flaws that prevent them from being effective, and of course Davidson is despicable and a clear representation of what happens when patriotism is pushed to its aggressive, paranoid extreme. Even Selver is imperfect, and must embrace terrible traits in order to save the Athsheans from eradication. The story is not a happy one, and none of the characters get a happy ending. Everything is irrevocably damaged by what happens between the Terrans and Athsheans, which is so realistic and believable it's almost painful to read. 
 And even though at the end the Athsheans win back their planet, even Selver notes that nothing will go back to how it was before. The nonviolent Athsehans learned violence, murder, in order to survive, and they cannot unlearn that. Was it worth it? The book doesn't answer that; it's a question Le Guin leaves with the reader, and one that is not easy to answer.

Set in rural Wisconsin, Shotgun Lovesongs tells the story of four men, and one woman, renegotiating the meaning of friendship, love and home. 
 Five characters share the narrative in alternating chapters. Hank - who inherited his father's farm, Beth - Hank's wife, Lee - an international music artist, Kip - a successful broker and Ronny -an injured rodeo star. These people speak and we think that we know them, who they are and what they dream of, but each are capable of surprising us as the story unfolds. 
 I have read few books that feature male friendship, and it was something that I really enjoyed about Shotgun Lovesongs. The bonds this group formed in childhood remain intact through a decade of physical separation and sporadic contact, but when they reunite in Little Wing they learn none of them are the boys they once were and their relationships with each other are now complicated by the men they have become. 
 The community of Little Wing in rural Wisconsin is vividly portrayed. I could easily imagine Kip's mill looming over the town, the car park full of battered pick-ups, weathered men leaning on the bar in the VWF hall and tractors traversing the the open farmland. 
 While tempers may flare, the conflict in Shotgun Lovesongs is largely personal and the drama is subdued. The pace of the story is measured and thoughtful, emphasising emotion over action. I found the writing and dialogue to be simple and honest yet descriptive and affecting. 
 Shotgun Lovesongs is an understated yet heartfelt novel, an ode to friendship, to love and to family. It is a story about finding your way home, where ever that may be.

A quick browse on Youtube revealed some really beautiful music and lyrics but I'm not a fan of his voice at all, I much prefer the covers by Adele {I Can't Make You Love Me} and Birdy {Skinny Love} for example, but play the clip below to sample his music.

There were lots of things I liked about Clariel, but this ended up being my least favourite of the Old Kingdom books. A prequel to the original trilogy, it follows the eponymous Clariel, as she is forced to live and enter into the politics of Belisaere, which leads to the endangerment of herself and her family. 
 I think my problem was that a lot of Clariel's qualities were exaggerated to the point of whininess. For instance, I thought it was really cool to have an asexual, or at least romantically disinterested, heroine: however, this quickly lost its novelty by being mentioned every time Clariel came into contact with a man, in great detail, and especially so when it descended into her simply being rude and dislikable. A similar thing happened with her desire to become a Borderer, it started as an admirable, interesting goal for her character, but was repeatedly referenced until it simply made her seem spoilt, selfish and whiny. I think this overstating of certain character traits becomes more obvious when you compare her with Sabriel, who had many of the same characteristics: a singular goal which she wants desperately, an apparent dislike of romance, the general need to fight, but whose character was more balanced overall, and ultimately still likeable. This difference may have something more to do with their respective character arcs overall, but before I realised the endpoint of Clariel's story it felt more like bad writing than anything else. 
 I also think the pacing of this book suffered quite a bit - it was very slow and, unlike Sabriel, did not have the virtue of a sequel to make up for its initial lethargy. Everything the happens in Clariel happens in the last quarter, or last half at best. It felt like the beginning was far too slow, and then the end was rushed, especially the culminating scenes. 
 Overall, I liked what this book tried to do, particularly with the avoidance of cliche female archetypes, but the execution, I felt, was pretty poor.

"God's wounds, Lada," he whispered, shaking his head. "Someday you will go further than I can follow." 
 Honestly, compared to last year's And I Darken, Now I Rise is a completely different beast. You know those series that just keep delivering and getting better as they go on? Yeah. I am in firm belief that The Conqueror's Saga is one of those series. It's truly something else. 
 "Hold hands with the devil until you are both over the bridge. 
 Or kill the devil and burn the bridge so no one can get to you." 
 Lada is more ambitious, more determined, more fierce than she was. She will do whatever it takes for Wallachia, and nothing will stop her. Her resolve and will throughout this book is damn near admirable. Her story, her determination to succeed and take back what's hers isn't new - not exactly - and I found myself often recalling the other journeys of characters to do similarly. (i.e. Daenerys from GoT, Aelin from ToG, Emily Kaldwin from Dishonored 2) Yet Lada blows all of them out of the water. This girl is made of pure and nasty grit, rage, anger and ambition - and damn, I kinda love her for it. It makes her storyline all the more compelling, anxiety-inducing and exciting. 
 She does things that are wrong, understands that, but also understands that it will bring her to her goal. She does not let herself consider the morality of the situation - Lada takes action and never inaction, no matter what. I've praised her characterization in the first book for being so... refreshing compared to most protagonists, but here she reaches a whole new level. It's absolutely fantastic. 
 "When you start lower, you have to fight for every scrap of space you occupy in the world... Even starting from nothing, I had more luck than you. If you had been born a boy, the whole world would tremble before you." 
 Throughout the story, Lada does some really unforgivable stuff, yet Kierstin White still manages to pull some sympathy into the reader. You understand why she does what she does, and no matter what - you still want her to succeed, regardless of the blood-strewn path she must carve to reach it. You know Lada's path is ugly, that she is going into a darker road, and her inevitable fate would likely be just as brutal - but that's the thing about this series, you're still empathetic. You care. I can't wait to see how White continues this trend in the next book. 
 Another reviewer, Simona Bartolotta points out how somehow, what could be a writing flaw with Lada ends up becoming a deeper introspection into her character and how she works. I don't want to elaborate, so by all means look at Simona's review. Just wanted to add that bit of knowledge to, if only to praise the book further. 
 "Today, he saw the true cost of two men's immovable wills. He saw what happened when men were forced to fight each other for months on end. It was not merely sickness of the body that plagued sieges, but sickness of the soul that turned men into monsters." 
 Shockingly, it isn't Lada's story that stole the show - it was Radu's. If you've read my review for the previous book, you probably know how much my heart bleeds for this child. Well. This book tore me apart because of his story. 
 Lada's tale may be about the people who start the wars, who take what they must; Radu's, on the other hand, is about those in the aftermath. Those who must survive the slaughter, who hold on to hope and wish and try to live, no matter what. Everything about Radu's storyline makes me cry, for it looks at war and siege in all it's ugliness and cruelty. It looks at how it can make monsters of men, how religion may sometimes be a crutch - or a reason, how it is not dying and preparing for the afterlife, but living in the current, how war affects everything and everyone. 
 Earlier this year, I also praised Vol. 7 of the Saga series for touching on this, but arguably, I'd say that this book was superior in discussing the themes of how tragic war can truly be. Regardless of which side you stand on, whether it be conqueror or survivor, it is still a cruelty. 
 Radu is caught between two sides. He is loyal to Mehmed, and his god - yet he is in the heart of Constantinople, living with the enemy and working with them - and he is torn. It's devastating to read about this plotline, absolutely painful and excruciating. It doesn't help that White's writing truly shines in it. 
 "He would die on the wall tonight, between his brothers and his enemies, because he could no longer distinguish between the two. They had finally come to the end. Whichever side won, neither would triumph." 
 With Radu is Nazira and Cyprian, two characters whom I absolutely adore with all my heart and soul. And honestly, this trio should be protected at all costs. They are too pure, too good, too kind for this world. They represent wishes, and hope, and fragile innocence, and love. They are the one true speck of light in this bleak, grey book. I don't even want to discuss further about them because it hurts to think about them, okay? Please, White. Allow us this. This one mercy, reunite them and let them retire someplace far away to heal.  
 "I cannot imagine a god who hates anything that is love, any way we find to take tender care of each other. I want you to find that same love, and I never want you to hate yourself for any love that is in you." 
 With Lada, meanwhile, is surrounded by her own group of allies(?). They're spectacular, each in their own way. Nicolae, in particular, shines in this book - with his good humor and eyes of hope compared to literally everyone else he's with. Yet, Nicolae isn't the only grand character in Lada's group (aside from the Dragon herself, of course). There are gems like Oana and Daciana, powerful women who serve well as foils to Lada herself. 
 If you haven't noticed, I refuse to talk about Mehmed. I didn't like him in book one, and I hated him in this one. Please tell me he dies in the last book.  
 Final note of praise is the world and setting. Kierstin White is masterful in bringing these historical settings to life, and equally masterful at writing historical events and religion - without being preachy or biased. It's stunning, and I applaud her so much for all the research and effort that came into respecting culture, history and belief, and reviving it all the same. 
 All in all, Now I Rise is a phenomenal sequel that is far better than its predecessor. It's also harsher, crueler, nastier and devastating, and I don't think the Dracul siblings' stories can be told in any other way. I can't wait for the third book. 
 If you haven't read the series or caught up, honestly, do yourself a favor and do so. It'll be so worth it.

Rating: / 2 conflicted stars. 
 Review: I'm conflicted, because while the book was interesting, it is definitely not all that it's promised to be or promoted. The majority of the book is consumed with the actions and movements of a constantly shifting war. And while, yes, this is important information and necessary to understanding the pressure and danger to these precious manuscripts, in the end, the books became a lesser thread in the story, only being mentioned sporadically. 
 The first third of the book was strong, the history and heritage of Mali, Timbuktu, and the wealth of knowledge preserved and dying within the crumbling books. We meet Haidara and his quest to find and compile the scattered manuscripts. His journey and the people he meets and the preservation effort are exactly what I was hoping and expecting from this book. 
 The rest of the book gives way to a very dry and factual account of Al Qaeda, politics, militants, and various news reports. It all becomes very journalistic and less like a story being told. And while we are updated at times to the librarians and books, they essentially fall behind and become nearly forgotten. It reads more like a nighttime news special. And all of this would be fine and interesting, except that the book is called The Bad-Ass Librarians of Timbuktu: And Their Race to Save the World's Most Precious Manuscripts...and we lose sight of the librarians. 
 When we finally return to the saving and smuggling, it is over too soon. I in no way want to downplay what was and is a very real situation, especially for those involved in saving all these manuscripts, but the author didn't give us enough. I wanted more first hand accounts from Haidara's family and even anonymous librarians and those involved inside Timbuktu. I recognize that the author can only give us what he is able to attain but perhaps more time was needed in assembling this book. At the very least, more first hand accounts from Haidara's nephew and chief assistant was needed. 
 The story of these librarians, preservationists, and citizens is nothing short of amazing. For that alone I am glad that I read this book. But overall I felt that this wasn't a successful book. I think you can see my conflict in reviewing this book. I'll leave it for other readers to decide for themselves, though, because while it didn't work for me, I know that others will find better than I did.

Written early 90s, at the beginning of the cyberpunk movement, a feminist jewish post-apocalyptic robot love story. After various nonspecific biological catastrophes (looks like climate change, rising seas, and various plagues) nation-states have all been replaced by corporations, menial workers try to survive in anarchic remains of megalopolises, and a few have independent towns protected by militias and competing corporate interests. Shira is a woman more defined by her personal relationships than her job, starting with the child her ex-husband takes away from her, and her childhood love, and the cyborg Yod. She's a bit of an empty shell; more interesting is Yod, questioning whether or not he counts as a person. And a Jewish one at that. Also Shira's grandmother, a feisty geriatric computer programmer, and Nili, an assassin from a distant isolated land. The world building is well done, including projections into cyberspace. Piercy does not trust her non-genre readers to pick up on conventions, most noticeably when she dumps a dictionary of slang into the text. There is also a substory of the life(?) of the historical Jewish golem in medieval Prague who is going through the same questions that Yod does. An interesting exploration of philosophical questions of existence, plus some good intermittent comments on feminism and sociology, like the sexual lives of older women.

Vinge is always one of the best writers at realistically depicting what the near future will really look like, at least in terms of information technology. This book posits a 2025 that seems pretty plausible to me. Given that Google Glass will be rolling out now, in 2014, and will probably get super popular pretty promptly, I don't think it's too outlandish to predict that we'll have information displays built into contact lenses in another 10 years, plus wearable computers controlled by minute gestures. Add to that extrapolations of the trends in entertainment, social networking, surveillance and nationalistic security apparati, and you get a future that Vinge paints as the world a famous poet finds himself in after he comes back from Alzheimer's, cured but not quite, by medical breakthroughs. As usual, this isn't great literature, but the writing isn't as bad as most science fiction, and there's some interesting and touching character development that makes it a bit more than a futurist manifesto.

And if I hadn't already read the book in the past, I'd rather watch the movie first Because, let's face it, the book is almost always better. So better to have my imagination somewhat pre-determined when reading the book than to have the book so fresh in mind as to be picking apart the movie without enjoying it. Better still to avoid getting sucked into three books in the first place, if it isn't going to be worth it. 
 It was worth it. 
 Immediately after watching the movie, I set about procuring the books from June, who'd mentioned she had them. I read them fast, in succession, all three, as non-stop as I could manage as the mother of two young boys with a pile of (a week's worth) of laundry to do, over the course of a few days. I will do my best to review them one at a time, without letting them blur too much. 
 I don't have to say that the books are engaging. The Hunger Games phenomenon wouldn't exist, otherwise. Katniss's cold pragmatism might have made her unrelatable as a protaganist, if not for the perfect backstory to secure our sympathies and not just explain, but justify her behavior. There were some world-building details that seemed false or excessive vague, but mostly in ways that were forgiveable for the sake of moving the story along for a young adult audience. 
 Most of the criticism of this book seems to lose sight of one important fact: Katniss was 16. By the end of most of the action in the third book, she's still only 17. So all of this "Katniss wasn't proactive enough," or "feminist enough," or somehow otherwise failed to personally destroy the entire mechanism of the Capitol all by her little lonesome in the first book is out of touch with reality. Or, at the very least, what it is to be a feminist character, book or film. 
 What makes Katniss remarkable is exactly what Peeta worries about on the eve of the Games. That she is always herself. She does not let them make her into something she is not. Even her "performance" in the caves, which seems out of character, is born out of both her pragmatism and her respect for the dignity of human life. 
 I am running out of things to say without spoilers. On to the next book!

I just finished reading this book for a second time. I rarely do that, but I have been lacking something good, and Kvothe has been on my mind a lot lately so I decided to give it a try. And it held up well. The fact that I would want to read a large tome like this a second time should mean something. 
 One of my goals is to get deeper inside the mysteries of this book. I know are a lot of questions going on in this book: trying to figure out what is happening in the present time, and trying to see how Kvothe's story brings him to the circumstances he is current in. As well as how his past has causes the present state of the world. 
 Rothfuss is a master story teller here -- you settle into his world, and he draws things in vivid colors. One of my favorite scenes is when he plays in the Eolian. Not sure I've ever read anything as good as that. 
  
 Upon this reading, I do believe that 75% of everything Rothfuss tells us about the Chandrian and the Amyr in Book 1 is in the beginning of the book, up to the point where Kvothe's parents are killed. Another 5% of the story is when Skarpi tells the stories in Tarbean. After that, Kvothe is after one goose chase after another. If your goal is learning more about the Chandrian and Amyr, closer studies should be given here. 
 If you read fairly closely, you will end up with more knowledge about the Chandrian and Amyr than even Kvothe-in-the-story has. This is part of Rothfuss' genius. 
  
 If you even mildly like fantasy stories, then I highly recommend this book to you. I have even been saying it's better than A Song of Ice and Fire and I still do mean that.

Sarah MacLean is one of those historical romance authors I've been wanting to read, but haven't had the chance to do so. When the opportunity came to participate in the blog tour, I knew this was my chance. MacLean's NO GOOD DUKE GOES UNPUNISHED is the third book in her The Rules of Scoundrels series. If you haven't read the series, it's perfectly safe to read NO GOOD DUKE without being exposed to spoilers. 
 As for characterization, it's a bit weak. I do believe it has to do with the fact that this is the third book in a series and some characters are already established. Our hero is Temple (William Harrow, the Duke of Lamont) who has spent the past twelve years known as Killer Duke. He has no memory of the night he met Mara Lowe and I just loved him! Your heart will be break when you realize that at times he thinks that maybe he did do the unthinkable and ah, he's just lovely. Then we have Mara and it's difficult to like her. She drugs Temple, withholds information, and you're just not sure what her overall agenda is. And when we finally get the truth you have to question if she's telling you everything. Even though I had a hard time liking her, her best moments are with the boys at the orphanage and with Lavender the pig. We have several secondary characters that make an appearance and play a small role. Mara's brother, Kit, is the reason why Mara has come out of hiding and let's just say he won't be going away quietly. Readers of the Rules of Scoundrels series will be happy catching up with past characters (ah Bourne is one that has me intrigued). 
 What I really enjoyed about MacLean's NO GOOD DUKE was the premise. I've read my share of historicals where the hero is often accused of murdering his wife or fiancee, but it's all speculation until the heroine comes and proves his innocence. In these novels, there's always a reason for the death and usually a villain to play it up. Here we don't and let me give MacLean a high-five for giving me a book that I've been waiting for! I just adore that we have the victim alive and well. It takes a while to get to the conflict and why Mara fakes her death, but when she does reveal everything you can't help but feel for her because her reasons are perfectly valid. I really liked that Mara owns up to her mistakes and eventually takes responsibility for it. 
 I debated with the rating between a three and four. Ultimately, I decided on four based on three factors. The first has to do with the premise which I've already explained that I really liked. The second is that this doesn't take place among the ton and the plot isn't dominated by the glittering ballrooms of the ton. Don't get me wrong, I adore historicals that feature these scenes because of the etiquette of the time and I love scenes with the hero and heroine sneaking outside for a private tete-a-tete. I most enjoyed getting a glimpse of another part of London-those featuring gentleman activities. And the final factor is the sizzling attraction between Temple and Mara. 
 Fans of historical romance will enjoy Sarah MacLean's NO GOOD DUKE GOES UNPUNISHED. I'm looking forward to reading MacLean's backlist and of course keeping an eye out for Chase's story.

This is my first Deanna Raybourn book. I was completely expecting it to be a terrible bore. Africa? In the 1920s? No supernatural elements? No sexy times? Colonialism? Ugh. Not for me. No, thanks. 
 It was great! Surprisingly, I really enjoyed the unique setting. Raybourn paints a very vivid picture of Africa. Africa really was a main character in this book. I was so surprised to find that Raybourn's Africa came from secondary sources. 
 I really liked Delilah as the lead character. I just instantly understood her character. Delilah is damaged and copes by living a life a frivolity and gaiety where nothing can touch her. Ryder is full of baggage, too. However, he copes by turning into a cold and unfeeling rock. I thoroughly enjoyed watching their struggles. 
 Raybourn catches a lot of flack for her portrayal of colonial Africa. I'm not sure I agree with that critique. I think she portrays different sides and experiences of colonialism to be read through a modern reader's eyes. For the most part, it works. However, I didn't like how Gideon was portrayed in a very Mammy-ish way. (Can a Southern female archetype be applied to an African male?) That did irritate me a bit, but not enough to hinder my enjoyment of the story.
Argh. I just found her self-absorbed and humorless. Enjoyed reading about the food and the scenery, but I'm mystified as to why this became such a bestseller...

 We Were Liars takes you on an epic and mysterious journey towards finding the truth of what happened in summer fifteen. The writing is metaphorical and poetic and the style is beautifully thought out to support the chaotic mess that is Cadence. There were moments when I had to stop and re-read certain paragraphs to let the feeling sink in and appreciate it at its fullest but not in a bad way (I always do this when I love the way an author phrased something). 
 I loved how E. Lockhart played with the style and broke apart sentences into different lines. Brilliant, although I understand it might annoy some people who don't like the meaning of such a simple, but efficient, way of portraying a character's personality and emotions. Things like these give me butterflies in my stomach because sometimes, a character is more than the words you are presented with; sometimes it's all about reading between the lines, fill up the voids and figure out the meaning of broken apart sentences. 
 However, as much as I loved the style, metaphors and the poetic feeling of the story, I had a hard time finding a connection with the characters. They came across as selfish, arrogant, naive (so, so, SO naive) and as stereotyped rich teenagers that I was so disappointed with them at first, although in hindsight, I kind of understand why they were acting the way they did but that wasn't good enough for me to accept them. 
 I suppose I could easily say this book was more plot driven than spending time on character development and for once, get ready for a shock, it's something that doesn't bother me at all now I have finished it. 
 Big gasp! 
 I was more captured with the mysteriousness of the whole story than its characters. Although I had figured out most of it by the time 'the truth' part began, I have to say that the hints were cleverly hidden and would have easily been read over if you just picked up the book knowing nothing about it except for the summary. 
 This book is perfect for a quick read between monster books and you still want something decent and challenging (plot-wise) to read. Overall, this deserves a four-point-five on the five stars' scale.

This book reels you in right from the beginning. The story is every mother's worse nightmare. A single mother takes her precious eight-year-old son to the park for a walk with the family dog. She gives him an ounce of independence and lets him walk ahead to get to a swing in the park. He's only out of her sight for a minute or two, but that's all it takes. When she gets to the swing, he's not there. The mother looks around frantically, but she can't find him. She asks friends and strangers who are at the park that day, but nobody saw him. The police are called, the missing child case becomes high profile, and people start pointing fingers. 
 The point of view alternates between Rachel (the mother) and Jim (one of the DI's investigating the case). Some of Jim's points of view are a therapy session that his department paid for hoping that it'll help him keep his job. The alternating POV adds suspense to the story and sometimes I had this desire to skip ahead because I couldn't wait to find out what happened next. What I loved most about the alternating POV was being able to see the story from a POV of a grieving mother and a frustrated DI. There are e-mail conversations and blog posts about the investigation, but I wasn't too fond of those, although I did see their importance -- these are the parts that I really wanted to skip. 
 There are many characters in this story other than the boy and his mother and every one of them is vivid -- even the minor characters are well developed in the short time they're in the story. There are plenty of screwed up characters in this book with traumatic pasts, so most of them look like a viable suspect. Some of the characters have long-held secrets that are revealed just when you think things can't get any worse. I felt so sorry for the mother. Her only child is missing and she's publicly falling apart at the seams. She appears unhinged, but who wouldn't in that situation? 
 I loved the fact that the story took center stage instead of the writing. The writing wasn't complicated, flashy, or distracting. The writing keeps the story going with plot and suspense and without drawing too much attention to itself. 
 I couldn't stop reading this book. I didn't know who was guilty, so I kept changing my mind. There were some nice misdirects, because several backstories intertwine with the missing child story. It was that wonderful rollercoaster ride of when I think a mystery is solved, but then I'm fooled and it's back to square one. I went back to my list of suspects, cross somebody off and then looked at the next person on the list. I was actually shocked at who was guilty. 
 If you love mysteries and thrillers with suspense, you'll love this one.
