Proposed new title: "It's Kind of an Okay Story". First of all, yikes. Transphobia much? When I saw that this book involved Craig meeting a transgendered girl while in the hospital, I assumed he was going to have a moment of enlightenment where he realizes, "Oh wow, I have been so very wrong. It turns out she is a person too, and I should stop being a jackass!" But no, instead Craig and Noelle persist in their jackassery, continually belittling the aforementioned girl, Jennifer. They refer to her as "Charles" and "he/him" instead of by her preferred name/pronoun. At one point they actually refer to her as "he/she/it". What is the deal? Not okay, Ned Vizzini. 
 Other things that bugged me: the style at the beginning of the book is really annoying. For instance, " 'Yo, yo,' my friend is like" is not a very well constructed sentence. I know it's supposed to reflect the way teenagers talk or something but this kid is supposed to be so brilliant that he gets into this ridiculously difficult school for smart kids. Why does he write so terribly? Incidentally, this style goes away for a long time in the middle of the book before coming back at the end. It was irritating then too, but I liked that I had a break from it. 
 Also, I took issue with the fact that Craig refers to the 5th edition of the DSM as the most common version out there and says that they're working on a 6th. Seeing as they're currently working on the 5th and the 4th is the most common one out there, this struck me as kind of a foolish inaccuracy, since he's supposed to be so fascinated with the DSM. At first, I thought this must be indicative of the book being set in the future or something, but if that was the case, then that was literally the only thing futuristic about this book. I know it's a stupid thing to get hung up on, but seriously, how hard would that have been to check/fix before publishing this book? 
 I didn't give this book only one star because it does have some redeeming features. Craig is pretty good about being kind to everyone (provided they aren't transgendered, of course) and also does a good job of speaking up when his friends/family are being overly stigmatizing. It was refreshing to get that in a character, since mental health issues tend to be cast aside a lot in our society. Also, I felt like the description of living with depression was very well done, it felt very real. However, this wasn't enough to make up for the other issues I had with the book. Hence, only 2 stars, and the second one is sort of grudgingly given.

 Cia's character really makes the book. She's extremely competent. 
 Cia is used to being the youngest. She has four older brothers and she has always been a year younger than every one in her class. So she's a little quiet, used to being talked over. But don't underestimate this girl. She's got the sharpest street smarts you may ever see in fiction. I was really impressed with how clever she is. She finds things to be suspicious about that I wouldn't even dream of. She takes her father's words seriously. You won't catch this chick lying down. She's a farm girl. Her expertise is mechanics and her knowledge of horticulture is not far behind. She values practicality, loyalty and simplicity. I liked her personality. A good mix of fierceness and kindness. 
 Tomas has always liked Cia but Cia has shied away from his attentions due to Tomas being a bit of a town celebrity with his looks and his brains. Cia has great respect for his brains. I did not. Mainly because the the author didn't give Tomas much of a chance to demonstrate said intellect. Tomas started out as a smart character but I feel the author dumbed him down a lot till he became a bumbling oaf that Cia has to struggle to keep alive. Do you know how unattractive that is? His role gets regulated to emotional support.

I get the feeling Moore had written 250+ pages, and then was like, "Where the heck do I go from here?" because it started to get rather dumb at that point. p.s. Lots o' f-bombs.

Well, that was an interesting piece of world building. I don't think it entirely worked, but you have to applaud the effort. 
 The gray semi-automatons of the Line are quite believable; made me think of the movie Brazil. The people of the Gun are a bit more of a stretch, especially as we learn just how they function. The Hill Folk left me thinking of some of Miyazaki's ghost people. 
 I'll try to be vague from here on, but there will be semi-spoiling. Be warned. 
 The half-made world is an interesting idea, but poorly explored. All we get is that once you're entering the unmade part, anything could happen. The sun rises in the west, trees walk ... yet oddly, the air is breathable and the not-quite-right creatures are edible. 
 I don't mind the telepathy of the Gun, but I could do without the remote healing and the infinite supply of ammunition. 
 The book's too long. Two-thirds the length would have sufficed to tell the story. 
 And the General? Well, darn it,  I knew about four pages after meeting him that we weren't going to find out his secret; not in this volume anyway.  That was frustrating. 
 I'll probably read #2 just to see where it goes. And I think Gilman's got a bright future.

I am so glad I re-read this book! I'd read it a few years ago and didn't really enjoy it then, but revisited it as a group read on the Georgette Heyer goodreads group. Now I include it among my favorites. 
 I love Alverstoke's reconstruction, the humor, the inclusion of two complex families (I think it's brilliant that Augusta pegs Frederica for Alverstoke straight off). 
 The only thing I didn't love was the declaration at the end. Occasionally Heyer disappoints here--pulling back and putting us in the head of a servant or, in this case, two interrupting brothers, when I want to savor the romance. 
 Frederica was such a fun mix of worldly practicality and unselfish devotion (which makes her a perfect match for Alverstoke I think), but I wish she'd been a little more in tune with her feelings. The part where Alverstoke explains to her what being in love with seemed to ingenue-ish for my conception of her. I think Frederica is smarter than that. She might feel love, deny it to herself, believe it impossible that Alverstoke would ever admire her, but--well, I would like her realization and the declaration better without the questions. So I'm going to black them out in my copy and begin at "I made up my mind years and years ago . . . " 
 And I'm getting rid of "Now I know! I am in love!" Frederica is too clever for that. Besides, I'd rather she kept kissing Alverstoke. 
 Whew. Sorry for being such a meddler. I'm curious though. Anyone else feel the same way?

 Marc's secret - he's a sexual dominant. He finds his girls at "Blue's" which caters to his cravings. It also a place where he could find a woman to fulfill his needs with no expectations and no promises. He can't have a relationship after Lily's betrayal and now, there's Chaili and her secretes. He knows she's a sexual submissive just by the look in her eyes when he "takes control" of the kiss. But, will she submit to him the way he needs her, why does she have that wall built around her, what are her secrets? Why is she so insecure? 
 Chaili's secrets - She likes it rough. Yes, she's sexually submissive but is not a submissive in the true sense of the word. She will never give up her freedom to a man, she will never allow a man to run her life, she has no want to be a slave - as her ex-husband expected her to be. She wants nothing more than to have a relationship with Marc, but she's afraid of what he will think of her, her needs and her body. 
 Marc and Chaili ... what a beautiful, heart-wrenching love story of two people who finally find each other but are afraid of what the other is hiding. Not only from themselves but from each other. When Chaili finally opens up to Marc and he realizes all that he has missed in her life, he makes it his mission to help her, love her and give her everything that she deserves. Especially the love and understanding of the man that she has loved most of her life. As he plays and sings "True Believer" to her, he realizes just how much she means to him and now it's time to get her to stop hiding, stop running from him and give him a chance. 
 I was blown-away by Beautiful Scars. Ms. Walker had me at "hello" as the old saying goes. I fell in love with Marc Archer in the first chapter. He was funny, loving and caring. She wrote a love story that takes your breath away and has tears in your eyes throughout the story for both of the main characters.

Carlos Ruiz Zafon is a talented writer and a miraculous self-promoter. The Angel's Game -- like The Shadow of the Wind -- will leave you convinced that you've read a better book than you have. But that doesn't mean you shouldn't read it. 
 In the case of TAG, the approach is fairly straightforward. Ruiz Zafon reverentially invokes the institution of Literature in all its forms, from a refuge for the young; to the pretentious journalistic elevation of copyediting into a sacred crusade; to the fucking smell of books; to the invocation of Dickens to canonize the institution of the blood- and melodrama-soaked potboiler. 
 This is all fine so far as it goes. Its real purpose is to telegraph what's about to come -- to create a theology of letters in which pulp holds a place of esteem no less dignified than nominally loftier stuff. Ruiz Zafon is going to give us pulp. He wants us to understand it to be exalted pulp. 
 I think this perspective is basically right. It reminds me of Michael Chabon's essays insisting that literature can include acts of imagination, excitement, adventure and the fantastic. As I steel myself for this year's Man Booker long list, it's good to be reminded that "good" books don't necessarily have to be about terminal illness and divorce. 
 Still, I do think that this framing is at least a little self-serving. Which is fine: Ruiz Zafon delivers a real page-turner, and ably adorns it with literary allusions and devices (albeit occasionally heavy-handed ones). The book has some problems with pacing, and the emotional pallette favors breadth over depth. But it's pretty great entertainment, ably weaving together thrills, supernatural horror, sexual tension, tragic romance, satire, noir and light comedy. 
 But I do worry that I will remember that this book is good more than I'll remember what the book is about. That's certainly the case with The Shadow of the Wind -- I remember where I read it, I and I remember liking it, but I remember terribly little of the book itself, which is pretty unusual for me. Perhaps TAG will fare better.

After trying to commit suicide after a particular nasty fight with her boyfriend, Death gives Lisa a choice: become Famine or die (sounds rather harsh, but it's not).  Lisa struggles with her anorexia, although she doesn't recognize it as such, she thinks she's just fat and has her very own Thin Voice to remind her of this. And of the calories everything edible holds and how much time on the exercise bike that accumulates to, to burn it off again. I thought this was so believable! Having no first-hand experience at having an eating disorder, I can imagine something inside whispering these deprecating thoughts. 
 One thing Lisa also struggles with, is hiding all of this from her boyfriend, best friend and father, the persons she cares about the most. At the start of the book she's already alienated her best friend because she told her to get help for her anorexia. Instead she gets a 'friend' who encourages her in her dysfunctional behaviour towards food: a girl with an eating disorder herself. 
 Death says things like 'thou art Famine, yo' and has a more than passing resemblance to Kurt Cobain, which is fine, but a bit weird. I did love the black horse, who Lisa names Midnight. The horse is sarcastic and doesn't get all the weird human behaviour. And it loves pralines, so it's my kind of horse. 
 I felt that what Lisa wanted most was to be in control of herself, not just being thin, but also in other aspects. She hates being bossed around, but doesn't really know what to do about it. 
 I'm glad that she learns to stand up for herself and that she's not worthless or undeserving of people's attention. 
 My rating: 4 stars, I'm looking forward to reading the sequel Rage.

For some reason, I always find it hard to write about the books I love. I know I love them, I just can't always seem to put into words why I love them. This is one of these books. I have read it about 3 or 4 times now, and it never fails to surprise me, I always find something new in it, and I am always hooked right up until the end. 
 The Name of the Wind tells the story of the notorious Kvothe (pronounce "Quothe"), who has given up his adventuring days to live a quite life as an innkeeper. When a historian called the Chronicler appears, noticing straight away who he is, Kvothe accepts the offer to tell the true story of his life. He agrees, on the condition that he gets three days to tell his story,The Name of the Wind is this first day. 
 Kvothe tells his story in chronological order, beginning with his tragic childhood in a troupe of travelling player, leaving him as an orphan. After spending years on the streets,he finally works his way to the University to study magic, where he is accepted at a young age. With no one to support him, Kvothe has to use his skills of lute playing to afford his tuition and survive. 
 Kvothe tells his story in chronological order, beginning with his childhood in a the Edema Ruh, a troupe of travelling players. The troupe acquire the scholar 'Abenthy', who trains Kvothe in scienve and sympathy (causing changes in one object by manipulating another). After witnessing Abenthy calling the wind as defence, Kvothe vows to discover the name of the wind in order to control it. Shortly after, Kvothe's father performs a song about the mythical Chandrian, which summons them and leads to them destroying the whole troupe, leaving only Kvothe alive. Orphaned and alone, Kvothe spends three years in Tarbean as a street urchin, developing his street smarts. He eventually approaches the University to continue his sympathy education. Despite passing the entrance exams, he is faced with continuous poverty and rivalry. In order to survive, Kvothe buys a lute and performs at taverns to earn money. 
 The story is not fast paced, but it is well paced, and has immense detail. It is thought provoking, and something is always happening, rather than everything all at once. We get to know Kvothe well, I personally, love him. If you are a lover of fantasy, then this is a must read. 
 Warning: every other book afterwards will seem dull, and insignificant in comparison.

3.5 stars. Sorry Natalie, I didn't love the book. 
 The best part of Unwind is the ideas. The debate it brings up is interesting and the moral philosophy kept me thinking. Unfortunately, this book felt like a clusterfuck of half-baked ideas focusing on all the wrong things. 
 The book centers around three main characters: Connor, Risa, and Lev (but mostly Connor). Connor and Risa are bland pieces of mayonnaise that I still don't know anything about, even after three hundred-something pages. The beginning centers mainly on Risa and Connor, but eventually shoves Risa aside and shines the spotlight on Connor. And boy, is he boring. 
 Okay, I'll admit: he does get more interesting as the book goes along. But I only want to get to know him a few chapters before the book ends. We barely know anything about him, and he avoids character development like the plague. We, the readers know very little about him. We've heard that he was a troublemaker in the past, but it's said throughout the book that he tries to stay out of the way of trouble. The heck? There's many possibilities for him to get the personality we so desperately want him to have, but it only happens three pages from the end. 
 Risa, the other main character, is said to be smart and that's about it. We know she plays the piano... cool? What are we supposed to do with that? Eventually anything that might've been considered interesting about her is shoved aside as she's made the Love Interest of Connor. Joy! Something major happens to her a few pages from the end of the book: she's paralyzed from the lower half of her body.  It's the most interesting thing to happen to her in the entire book, and it's blown over. So much could've come from that, but it's tossed out the window like the rest of my hopes and dreams. 
 Easily the most interesting character in the book is Lev. He has the most personality, development, and charisma than Risa and Connor combined. It's with him we learn the most about the world this takes place in, the legal and moral repercussions, and the damage Unwinding causes to kids. It's with him we meet Cy-Fi, who is honestly the coolest, most complex, and smartest character in the entire book. Without Lev, this book would be a steaming dumpster fire of boredom. Unwind would've instantly been much better if the plot focused on Lev and instead made Connor and Risa side characters. 
 Onto the plot: frankly, there wasn't too much. The book probably could've started halfway through and would've still had the same message, just a lot more concisely. Things only get interesting when they reach the Graveyard. In general, the plot felt slow, unfocused, jumpy, and underdeveloped. The most interesting part of this book was the debates that occurred, and those didn't get started until about halfway through. The thing I loved the most hands-down had to be the subplot with the Admiral's son. The scene with every part of his Harlan "reuniting" was touching, and I wish there had been more scenes like it. The only other part of the book that could compare was Cy-Ty, begging his family not to Unwind him. Those two scenes were the core of the book.  If there had been more scenes like those, the book I'm currently reviewing would be a lot more hard-hitting and emotional. 
 TL;DR, this book was a bit of a mess with some shiny bits. I'm hoping the series improves as it goes on, since I'm probably going to be pressured into reading the next one.

 I've known pain my whole life, but this is a new kind for me. It isn't born of something wrong or ugly. This pain is conceived out of beauty - my love for Jack Henry McLaughlan. I embrace it. I clutch it as tightly as I can with both fists because I never want to forget the love I have for him. Loving him will forever be my Beauty from Pain. 
 I want to make this review short and to the point, so I can get right to the next book!!! I have to say I really liked it!!! It started out kind of iffy at first. In fact, for the first half of the book, I was thinking meh..., but just beyond the halfway mark, it really took off for me. I don't know if I just got used to the characters, or they just started getting less annoying. But either way, I was glued to the pages, and couldn't put it down!!!!! 
 The premise of the story is not a new one, it is a classic young millionaire, trying to remain anonymous, seeking companionship from an unknown... and I mean really unknown woman (like fake names etc.) This one takes place in Australia, so it has a little Aussie culture mixed in. And even though the storyline is a bit cliche, it still kept my interest and actually turned out to be quite intriguing!!!!! 
 Jack McLaughlan, a 30 year old Australian wine mogul and millionaire has decided that anonymous, short-term relationships will be the only option he has for companionship and intimacy in his life. He has ruled out love and family based on his past and apparently bad experiences, and has limited these relationships to three to four weeks at max. Real names are absolutely withheld to preserve his privacy, and full disclosure and steadfast agreements for finite time frames has become his way of life. 
 Laurelyn Prescott is a 22-year-old musician, visiting Australia from America with her best friend Addison. With this visit, Laurelyn is attempting to gain some piece of mind following a recent brake-up, when her boyfriend and record producer turned out to be a married man with children. Laurelyn, herself being an illegitimate child of a famous country music star, feels completely betrayed by this new knowledge, and is NOT the least bit anxious to start another new relationship with any man. But she doesn't hold out long. 
 Jack encounters Laurelyn at a nightclub in Wagga Wagga, on the night of her arrival, and decides for all intents and purposes that she will be his next subject. And it is not long before he makes his play. Laurelyn was not only intrigued with him, but was also completely ON BOARD with his proposal, after only a day of contemplation. I was a bit let down by her coy behavior regarding this agreement and then her quick submission. It was obvious she wanted to do it, yet it seemed to me, she played a few games trying to make him "work a little harder for it." 
 But in the end the two had amazing chemistry together. Not only instant attraction, they also had an ease about them they just made their relationship work. The sex was volatile and hot as fuck, but the intimacy was even more intense. They shared feelings with each other easily and bonded quickly. Jack was sweet and considerate, and quite consistent. And Laurenlyn was not only drawn to Jack physically, but was also connecting with him in ways that she had never experienced before. 
 I had to admit, I was completely surprised by the level of devotion Jack showed towards her. In fact, based on his past history, it was almost not believable. Jack was just completely swoon-worthy, and when I was expecting arrogant asshole, I got a loving, devoted partner. And Laurelyn, while she started out as coy and playing games, she ended up quite levelheaded and genuine. But again, this was an arranged relationship, scheduled to end after 3 months time. 
 But right from the start, Jack found he was breaking his own rules, and you just knew that these two were going to make a connection that was going to be unbreakable. I knew it, they knew, and NO ONE did anything about it. And that pissed me the fuck off!!!!!!!! She was in LOVE with him, he was in LOVE with her... but didn't realize it until it was TOO FUCKING LATE!!!!!! 
 Jack, you don't always know the true worth of a woman's love until it becomes a memory." 
 Yes a little predictable but still nothing less than ADDICTIVE!!!!! Now, I have to know what happens next.... So I'm on to book two. Sorry, but I'm ending it here so I can get TO IT!!!!!! 
 So, if you like 30 year old millionaires, damaged but redeemable heroines, and sex scenes that are smoldering HOT... this is the book for you!!!!!!! 
 Highly recommended romance!!!!!!

 Heir of Fire promised to be excellent based on the previous two books. However, it ended up being a disappointment. 
 I don't quite know what it was, but it took me longer to finish it, for instance. Maybe because the pace was extremely slow at first. With a setting far from Adarlan and everything exciting that had happened in Crown of Midnight out of the way, as I read it, I just felt like Celaena baking on top of a rooftop - sluggish, drunk and lost. 
 This series was like your average romantic relationship: it started so well, so gripping and so swooning, I couldn't put it down. And then came the "we've-seen-and-done-it-all-so-what-now" phase. This book was a bit messy. It was boring at places, picking up my interest here and there, building my hopefulness only to have it thrashed again. Even when it was getting really good, it never became great. The climaxes were not up to my expectations. Not after such wonderful precedents. 
 First of all, there was no Chaol. There was no awesome plot unfolding at hallucinating speeds, leaving you breathless and gasping for more. No romance. No "holy shit, I can't believe this happened now!". Celaena barely spared a thought at what she had left behind, and became a completely different person. It was like she didn't even care and it was soooo infuriating. I just kept wondering what had happened to her - even though Maas hints that she's just depressed or something, I couldn't quite buy that. 
 And then, her relationship with Rowan. I was praying they would not get involved romantically and just spoil everything. Because they had a really nice friendship, sweet and cute comradie, but hardly any chemistry. Not like the one she had with the Captain. It was great, it was different, but it was not romantic. In the end, I couldn't even understand what they truly were. I can only hope against all hope Maas won't turn it around in Queen of Shadows. 
 Thirdly, the POV-switching. It was always cool to switch to other characters' perspectives and see what they were thinking. But they were characters we already knew something about or were at least interested in knowing what they were up to. The witches were just a complete WTF for me. I didn't get why we had to have a new character to follow, when I (and I think a lot of people would agree with me - or not) was a lot more interested in what would happen in Wendlyn or Adarlan. Nobody cared about the witches! 
 It became extremely anticlimactic when it happened. Because although Manon became somewhat more balanced, she was still not up to pair with everything else I had experienced in this series. Her whole coven and history was not particularly gripping, either. They were the emos of the whole thing, and never became anything else. 
 I did enjoy when Abraxos came into the picture, and that first moment of them was amazing. It reminded me so much of How to Train Your Dragon, and it was adorable and painful for me at an emotional level. But the fact of the matter is, I wasn't interested in Manon - I was interested in her wyvern, most of the time. Which is not ideal when so much of the book revolves around her and her story in the mountains. Sometimes it became interesting, but not enough, and never led anywhere. I get that she was born without a heart or a soul, but goddamn it, just stop being so insufferable and get your head out of your ass! 
 Bottom line, I couldn't care less about her. 
 Not only did the structure change in this book, but also the language. It became a lot more vulgar than before, which doesn't bother me too much. It's just that it feels like someone else is writing it at times. 
 The characters became quite bland and uninteresting, especially Celaena and Chaol, whom I treasured the most. It was like they'd lost their raw identity in favor of other lesser things. It made no sense. Like a lot of plot devices in this book, and that explained events that had occurred in the previous books. I felt like Maas kept trying to explain why so and so had to be done a certain way to lead to so and so outcome, and even she couldn't quite grasp the meaning of it. Because it made no freaking sense. 
 Like the Nehemia arc. I didn't feel any sort of connection towards the princess, and didn't feel like Celaena had either. In the end, I kept questioning when had they become best friends. I didn't remember it happening! It was just so strange. Like Maas had suddenly decided Nehemia was to become a plot device so big it would shatter everything else the reader believed in. It did shatter something in me, but it was not what she intended, I think. She didn't allow enough time for that relationship and that notion to settle. It was too rushed. And it didn't get any better in this book. 
 I did like the little plot twists and touches here and there, even if most were predictable enough. Don't get me started on the carranam one, though. That was just painful. Sugary sweet and painful. 
 Still a fine book for Throne of Glass fans to read, but it felt more like a filler than anything else. It was not as "wow" as the previous books. It would never have been, I think, based on all the changes Maas has decided to make. What was she thinking? 
 Still, I give it 3 stars. Call it bias - it probably is - but I did like this book anyway, even if I kept reading it mostly to find out what happened next rather than to enjoy what was happening. Which is a bit sad, but it's not my fault! I adored Throne of Glass and Crown of Midnight. And just as I would not give up on a long-term relationship that was deteriorating fast, I will not give up on this series. Because it and I are very much attached and in love. 
 Goddamn you, Heir of Fire.

 Laureth (which is a name I really like) is blind but if you would walk up to her on the street I can bet you you'd never know. She's that good at faking the fact she can't see and it makes me really admire her, as a person. The confidence she has, for someone with a disability or not, is astonishing and not to mention the bravery. She goes off to New York, on a whim, because she's worried about her father. Takes her little, adorable brother Benjamin, and is off like it's no big deal. 
 Benjamin is one of the most enjoyable characters in this book, not that the others aren't fantastic characters. He's just this adorable, innocent seven year old kid who is so mature beyond his years. If you have any siblings, especially younger, reading about Benjamin just wishes your sibling was more like him when you were younger (or even now). I especially love his relationship with his stuffed Raven, Stan and electronics. 
 This is one of those books that will get you thinking. That will make you want to pay attention to all the words you're reading. Heck, it's one of those books that will make you want to go back and read it again after you've finished to catching everything you've missed. Everything about this book is just brilliant. The visualization, the characters, the co-inky-dinks, the number obsession (which will blow your mind when you realize just how in-depth it is) . . . just . . . everything.

As ever, this reader is a sucker for a marriage of convenience--regardless of the era. 
 Characterization and character development would have to be the most standout elements of this story. I'd be tempted to call it a sort of Ugly Duckling tale, but the heroine doesn't become a ravishing beauty at any point--only reforms her sense of style and self-confidence as she finally thrives after years of physical and emotional neglect. And as a genuinely interesting twist, the hero is blind. Motivations are understandable all the way around, and the chemistry between the two is both organic and believable. 
 I struggled for a while over the rating. The prose and structuring had me hovering at 3 1/2 stars through most of the book, as the pacing came off as a bit languid and slow at some points. I also wasn't clear on the hero's past history with women, and the question of whether he had experience with intimacy or not never seemed to clear up for me. (Please, someone correct me or point me back to a chapter/passage if I missed something!) But given the consistent theme threading, the satisfying ending, and the author's bravery in tackling the hero's impairment, I decided my enjoyment level felt 4-star appropriate. 
 From the very beginning, I loved the idea of this story and the damaged state of both the hero and heroine. And I believe most readers will be able to achieve empathy without pity. The story introduces us to other interesting members of the "Survivors Club," which surely gives readers future options to follow. I know I'll be hanging on to this one, and possibly seeking out one or two of the interconnected stories.

Over the past few years, my eyes had often lingered over this book by chance at the bookstore. The title's just so attention-grabbing that it had a lot of pull on my interest, as did the premise. I have a bit of a weak spot for stories set in boarding schools. 
 Underneath its prestigious facade, the Gallagher Academy's training students to be spies. Traditional math, English and history have no part in their school schedules; a Gallagher Girl's coursework consists of hacking government computers, conducting surveillance, and combative techniques, to name a few typical class tasks. All girls are skilled athletically and academically--outsiders are only half-right in their assumption that Gallagher Academy is for snooty geniuses. These girls can converse in fourteen languages and are advanced in other such cerebric tasks which our main character tends to mention in asides to the reader. 
 Speaking of our main character, her name's Cameron Morgan, or Cammie "the Chameleon", so-called because she has the innate ability to blend in with the backdrop of everyday life when an operation's being conducted. She's actually the daughter of the headmistress, but she gets no special treatment and is pretty much just like any other Gallagher Girl at school, with one differential exception: She's not removed from the awareness that there's a danger the espionage lifestyle can bring with it, a danger that's brought grief to her family. 
 At the end of a practical test doing spywork for her teacher, our Chameleon stands out for the first time. It's not just anyone who notices her, it's a boy. (Specifically a cute boy. Of course. This is a work of fiction, you know!) Their encounter plays on Cammie's mind and eventually leads to her crafting a normal persona in order to date him, with a lot of help from her friends (you know you've got true friends when they accompany you to stake out a guy's house and hijack his e-mails!) Cammie's interest in Josh is more than just that of any all-girls school student connecting with a boy for the first time: Josh represents the outside life she never had, that of normalcy. But can she continue pretending she's as normal as he is, when that's so far from her reality? 
 At best, I hoped this would be a cute fun read; no expectations, just hoping it wouldn't be unlikeable, and I do think it succeeded. The dialogue is funny at times and not in a tryhard way like in some teen books; it seemed like it came naturally rather than pulled from an "Author's List of Funny Quotes to Box Into Book Somehow". Less natural to me were most of the moments meant to amp up the drama, and some other plot occurrences when it felt like the author was at Point A. and knew she needed to get to Point C. but didn't know how to end up there, so made things convenient for herself. An example of this would be Cameron and her friends out driving when it just-so-happens that Josh is walking past. That's a bit more than coincidental, for it to be him of all people at that exact moment. 
 I appreciated how the author balanced reader accessibility with still getting across the fact that these girls are geniuses, without breaking immersion. Cameron casually refers to topics that are common knowledge for the girls, and it shows enough of what they know in relation to academia. I think it works. Also well done is the imagination in this spy world; the classes themselves, the inventions that they use in day-to-day school life, and the tidbits of Gallagher Girl history (your history class taught you that so-and-so contributed this to society? Nope, that was actually a Gallagher Girl, but it was covered up so shhh.) 
 At times it seemed the book had much more of a younger tone than the high school age it was meant to depict. The characterization carries that feel, as well, with the way they acted and the blandness to the characters. I didn't care about any of them when all's said and done. It may be this that made me divided on where I sat with my enjoyment of the book sometimes during my reading, but I can say I landed on the more favorable side so I'm going to check out the next book. Hopefully I'll remain of favorable opinion throughout, because I've read that the series starts out more ligthearted but at some point shit starts to get real, so I want to see what was meant by that.

I really enjoyed Also Known As earlier in 2013, so when I saw this digital ARC pop up on Netgalley I knew I needed to read it. Going Rogue did not disappoint! I will say, though, that if you haven't read Also Known As, you should definitely read that one first. While Benway does take some time in Going Rogue to recap what happened previously, it's not really enough to give you the whole feel for the first book. 
 Maggie is not your typical teenage girl, no matter how much she wants to be, because you just can't have secret super spy parents and be one of the world's best safecrackers and consider yourself normal. I appreciate her desire to have a normal life, though, and she gets it to some extent with her best friend, Roux, and her boyfriend, Jesse. It's just that she also spends hours crammed into tiny crawlspaces in international criminals' houses. Tiny detail. 
 What I like about this series is that it's realistic in its characters, but the circumstances are fantastical. I mean, no... it's probably not real life-like that these things happen to Maggie and her family and her friends, but their reactions to the situations feel real. That's what I like in a book - normal people in abnormal circumstances.  This book. Oh my gosh this book! It was so so so good and such a worthy follow up to the awesome that was Splintered. I love love love this Alice in Wonderland retelling. From the world to the action to the characters, everything about it is just fantastic. There are so many twists and turns and I never see anything coming. I loved every single second of this book. I started reading it before bed one night and ended up staying up all night to finish it because I was addicted. 
 Alyssa is such a wonderful heroine. I love her! I love her because she is strong but still afraid but courageous in spite of that fear. She tries to ignore her responsibilities and be normal, but you can't even fault her for doing so. It's scary and life would be easier if she didn't have to deal with any of the nonsense. But when push comes to shove, she does what needs to be done. This book sees Alyssa discover herself. She transforms a great deal over the course of this book. She has to come to terms with her netherling side, while still keeping touch with her human one. It's not an easy thing to balance, but Alyssa does her best. 
 Then there is Jeb and I have such a soft spot for Jeb. He really is incredibly sweet and kind and clearly loves Alyssa with all his heart. I love their sweet moments together and I love their relationship. It was so hard to see Jeb not knowing Alyssa's true side or remembering any of the crazy things they did. 
 Then there is Morpheus and I will admit it, I have a blind spot a mile wide when it comes to Morpheus. I pretty much overlook anything he does mostly because underneath it all there are good intentions there. He is, hands down, my favorite character in the books, if not one of my favorite characters ever. I want him and Alyssa to get a happily ever after in the worst way possible. I love their relationship because they stand on equal footing. He is always pushing Alyssa to be stronger because he knows she is. He knows she is capable of greatness and he wants to see her shine. "Game, set, match. Ever, and always, my equal." Morpheus is darkly charming and manipulative at times and he is not your normal hero, but I love him all the same. "There is nothing black and white about Morpheus. He's a chaotic portrait made of every shade of gray." 
 This is how you know it is a wonderful love triangle, because I have nothing but good things to say about both love interests. Don't get me wrong, I'm backing Morpheus 100% but I have no desire to see Jeb hurt. I read the books rooting for Morpheus and wanting him to win. However, at the same time when something happens to threaten Jeb and Alyssa's relationship, it still makes my heart hurt. I love them both and I can see how Alyssa could be torn and that is what makes the love triangle work. 
 Like Splintered, the plot in Unhinged takes twists and turns the entire time. I love characters and then I hate them and then characters I hated I end up loving. I never know where I stand with these books and that makes them fantastic. I never know who is pulling the strings and who is just a puppet. I love a book that keeps me on my toes. Unhinged takes the madness that is Wonderland and brings it into our world. And while I did miss taking a trip through Wonderland, it was also awesome to see Wonderland seep into our world. It also added the drama of hiding the madness from the rest of the world. Not such an easy thing to do. 
 The ending to Unhinged left me dying for more and waiting for Ensnared is going to drive me mad. I absolutely loved the journey that was Unhinged. I got another wild ride, a ton more Morpheus, more Wonderland madness, and no middle book syndrome to be found. I could not have asked for more from this sequel.

A.A. Dark has taken Dark to an entirely different level. This story will have your stomach in a perpetual state of knots. And this is definitely not for the faint of heart. I'm used to dark novels, and I can say this story is the most disturbing one I've ever read. It will emotionally punch you in the stomach with the horrors Everleigh goes through. 
 I kept waiting-needing to seeing the light at the end of the tunnel, and yet the physical abuse, (graphic) rape, and emotional manipulation continued to plague Everleigh throughout the entire novel. There was no end to it, and not an HEA in this book, but we're left with a to be continued. I was left feeling emotionally drained with no sense of peace at the end, and I'm not sure how I feel about it. 
 What I had seen. What had been done to me, and what I had done, somehow made a permanent stain on my mind. And the horrors weren't over. They'd never end... 
 Bram the owner of Whitlock, a large underground slave community that caters to the rich and famous' sadistic fantasies where Everleigh has been kept for the last fourteen years is in love with her. I found it more of an obsession than love. No matter how sick you are, you don't physically abuse or watch someone else abuse someone you love. He does both. 
 I hated how Bram was romanticized. 
 The Butterfly Garden deals with a similar captivity story. And what it does really well is not romanticize the male lead. Instead, he is looked at like a coward for the letting the evils continue. I loved the message it sent, and the fact it wasn't justifying someone's actions because he seemed to be nice on occasion. 
 In 24690, Everleigh's twisted and brainwashed thoughts empathize with Bram. She believes he's a good man because he doesn't believe in pedophilia. She makes excuses for him in her head that make him sound like a decent human being. He OWNS a freakin human trafficking community where he allows absolute monstrosities to occur. But to her, he was cleaning the place up after his father left it to him, and making it a better place. The only better place a slave community could be is not a damn slave community. 
 I don't like the romance part of it, and I'm hesitant to read the second because I'm scared of the road it's going to go down. 
 I don't empathize with Bram, nor do I care for him in the slightest. Not a good situation for a romance. But good thing that was such a small part of the book. 
 The majority of the story carries you through the atrocities Everleigh encounters, and conflict with Bram's friend West. West is jealous of everything Bram has, Whitlock and Everleigh included and he'll stop at nothing to see that he gets it. 
 The thing about this story is it's told in three POVs, allowing you insight into a twisted slave's mind, a man who had a dark future pushed on him, and a monster to the highest degree. It's a mindf*ck being in their minds and trying to understand what's right. Is Bram redeemable because this dark destiny was pushed and beat into him from childhood? Is there some humanity to West that we should care about him? Are Everleigh's feelings for Bram real or a sense of Stockholm Syndrome? 
 This was a sick and twisted story, with very graphic scenes of rape, abuse, human mutilation, and emotional manipulation. Make sure you're in the right mindset and prepared to be disturbed.

What did I think of this book? 
 It's tough to say. 
 On one end, mostly the beginning, it's short, with not enough juice in the though process of our heroine. But when our heroine gets kick-ass, then things tend to get interesting. Sadly, it didn't happen often. 
 Half the time, she rushes into battle with no reason. Well, she says she has a reason, but it doesn't quite resonate. Not everyone can relate to pure hatred and blood lust (not the actual kind), but it's trying to communicate an idea I didn't even understand, much less connect with. 
 A lot of the events that happened didn't get their allotted time slot in the actual text. Some elements were better off being said out of dialogue. 
 And my God, the dialogue! 
 I desperately want to say that it was great, because some of it was pure genius. The quirky one-liners and the sarcasm. It's like a dream come true for someone like me. But it did have it's downfalls. A lot of the characters came across as rant-y. They would say the same thing over and over in one shot, with not enough meat in between to chew on. Like, really? You're gonna tell everyone the state of your sex life to a guy you just met, who just tried to kill you? 
 Honestly, the elements in this book didn't really work together. I don't know what it was, the writing or the dialogue or the ideas themselves, but whenever I try to solve it, I get the ERROR message. Whilst reading it, I felt contradicted half the time, on the world building, and the other, I tried to figure out the motives of Cat and Bones. Like I said, the elements would be there, just with no reasonable connections.

 Between the World and Me is my first Ta-Nehisi Coates book, and I was assigned this book for one of my classes is Critical Diversity Studies. This book is, essentially, a letter written by an African American father, to his teenage son, who appears to be finally seeing the injustice and violence on Black young men, specifically by law enforcement. 
 As someone who grew up during the time Coates grew up, I found myself all too familiar with his references and the need he felt to behave a certain way as a form of protection from the streets. The criticisms of this book being too self-defeating are valid, yet at the same time, as the author says in the book, the parents of Black children are fearful; fearful of the streets and fearful of law enforcements. One cannot argue that being a young, Black man in America is not a struggle in itself that others will never be able to completely relate to. I enjoyed the book and I enjoyed Coates' writing, his honesty, and his candidness. I was a dismayed at times by his advice to his son, that essentially, nothing is going to change, and racism will always be the way it is - but I understand how someone can have that opinion given the journey he has been on. I also felt that his opportunities to succeed academically were not taken advantage of, and it felt as though he made excuses for that; let's face it, if you have an opportunity to graduate from Howard University, you TAKE it. 
 I specifically enjoyed the meeting he had with his college friend's mother about the death of her son and how graceful and regal she still seemed to be. She seemed like the type of woman who did not let the institutional and structural racism of her time period effect her successes and triumphs. I felt like he could have learned a thing or two from someone like her. 
 All around, good book.

Are You Ready to Romp Through the Apocalypse? 
 The Perfect Summer Read 
 Are you looking for a fun, quirky book to read? Good Omens: The Nice and Accurate Prophecies of Agnes Nutter, Witchby Terry Pratchett and Neil Gaiman is an oldie but goody. 
 If it's an oldie, why write a review? 
 Because I keep running into people who haven't read this gem, and most of all, because I love this book. The satire is at once silly and hysterical with some honest-to-goodness wit thrown into the mix. It's a zany romp that only the young at heart should take. There's enough British wit and humor to satisfy anyone who likes that sort of thing, and it's genuinely crazy enough to amuse most people. If you're a Douglas Adams fan, well, then you've probably read Good Omens. 
 Warning: if you have no sense of humor or if you hate silly, stop reading this review. 
 Brief Summary: 
 Satan and God have a huge problem: the Antichrist has gone missing, and they need him for the apocalypse. It turns out that when the lad was born, some evil nuns gave him to the wrong couple, and he grew up in a sleepy English suburb. Expect for his untapped "evil" power, he's an ordinary kid rather like Kevin McCallister, the kid in Home Alone . 
 Because they happen to like earth and don't want it destroyed, Aziraphale (an angel) and Crowley (a demon) team up to stop the apocalypse; they are much like a British version of the Odd Couple who are trying to save the world from inevitable doom--Crowley, of course, lives life wildly and fully, while Aziraphale is quiet and refined. While everyone (God, Satan, angels, demons, and humans) searches for the Antichrist, the Four "Bikers" of the Apocalypse gather. And, yes, the Prophecies of Agnes Nutter, Witch are important. 
 Pratchett and Gaiman have created a diverse and eccentric cast of characters. The impending doom is told through multiple points of view as everyone races to save or destroy the world. As any reader would expect, they all come crashing together at the end of the book. 
 Why do I like it? 
 This may be one of the funniest books I've read. First, Pratchett and Gaiman turn the story of the apocalypse inside-out, then, they turn it sideways, and finally, they manage to make the end of the world riotous and entertaining. Along the way, they poke and prod at the ordinary, the crass, and the sacred. 
 I'll admit there is a great deal of silliness about the book, and some of the motifs have been used before, but Gaiman and Pratchett take those motifs and spin them with enduring flare. After all, the book was published in 1990 and is still going strong. 
 I'm always excited when someone I know reads Good Omens for the first time. 
 So my friend, take a break from the real world, put aside all serious thoughts, get comfortable, and read this delicious book.

 Hannu Rajaniemi must be one of the most creative and ambitious science fiction writers in our era, and his imagination is fully displayed in the whimsical, imaginative, and often downright peculiar stories of the collection. In fact, to echo that motif, I'll start with the last two sections, in which his experimental streak is most prominent. The first, "Snow White is Dead," is intended to be an interactive neurofiction experience: machine learning algorithms used feedback from an electroencephalography headset to lead the reader on a subconscious choose-your-own-adventure story. The second section is a collection what Rajaniemi terms "microfiction:" each microstory must convey the bones of the plot and scene in under 140 characters. The microstory starring Imhotep Austin became a serial. One of my favourite episodes: 
 "Kidnappings, impossibly aged bodies, green chronal energy dome in Brooklyn. Routine case--for a half-mummy detective. But now it's personal." 
 In fact, given Rajaniemi's gift for fantastic first sentences, I suspect that many of the stories in this collection are microstories given flesh and substance. Almost all of them begin by concatenating two startling and apparently incompatible events that automatically pique the reader's curiosity. Every single such sentence is in fact a perfect summary of events while simultaneously expressing nothing about the story's essence. Take "Tyche and the Ants": 
 "The ants arrived on the Moon on the same day Tyche went through the Secret Door to give a ruby to the Magician." 
 The story is an odd melding of myth (Tyche's friends on the moon include Chang'e and the Jade Rabbit), technology (the aforementioned ants are of the ANT-A3972 variety), and the dreams of childhood. Similarly, the first sentence of "The Haunting of Apollo A7LB" ("The moon suit came back to Hazel the same night Pete was buried at sea") manages to both fully describe the plot while not even alluding to the core of a story about love and loss and racism. "The Server and the Dragon" ("In the beginning, before it was a Creator and a dragon, the server was alone.") is slow-paced and contemplative, and explores what it might mean to be a server isolated from the world of information it feels compelled to serve. While not my favourite in the collection, I savoured that first sentence and the contrast between dancing dragons and baby universes. 
 Rajaniemi's stories are often bewildering, catapulting the reader in the middle of an intricate world whose rules can only partially be gleaned from the story. One of the most obvious examples of this was "His Master's Voice" ("Before the concert, we steal the master's head.") which is narrated by a dog. A hyperintelligent dog, I grant you, but a dog nonetheless. Rajaniemi does a wonderful job in capturing the essential dogginess of the perspective, creating a voice that muses on his master's "god-smell" and the great triumvirate: the bowl, the Ball, and the master. The first story in the collection, "Deus Ex Homine," opens with an energy and incredibly alien imagined future that is carried through the story: 
 "As gods go, I wasn't one of the holier-than-thou, dying-for-your-sins variety. I was a full-blown transhuman deity with a liquid metal body, an external brain, clouds of self-replicating utility fog to do my bidding and a recursively self-improving AI slaved to my volition." 
 The story is told by one of the casualties of the "godplague," a phenomenon in which humans, in becoming something more than human, wreaked havoc upon civilization. As one character notes, 
 "Recursively self-optimizing AIs don't kill people. Killer cyborgs kill people." 
 Like other Rajaniemi stories, I was initially overwhelmed by the strangeness and complexity of the world, but was inexorably sucked into the story nevertheless. I was glad that Rajaniemi returned to the world of the godplague in another story in the collection, "Elegy for a Young Elk," which also highlights his fondness for flashbacks. It gives the perspective of another type of casualty, a poet who refuses to become transhuman but loses his family to the godplague and its aftermath. 
 Rajaniemi is one of the few authors that makes me regret my lack of knowledge about physics. Although I spent a certain amount of time on wikipedia learning what WIMPS and Shkadov neclaces were, a lot of the references flew past me. One such story was "Invisible Planets," a series of brief glimpses of bizzare worlds tenuously connected by a conversation between a darkship and one of its subminds. All the same, I enjoyed the vignettes, which, as the darkship notes, 
 "Are each defined not by what you speak of but by what is left unsaid." 
 The technological allusions of "Skywalker of Earth" ("Twelve hours before the rain of ships.") were also lost on me. Skywalker, the longest story of the collection by far, was almost reminiscent of a Professor Challenger adventure story if it could be transformed into modern hard science fiction.  
 While I found the story a bit of a drag at times, I absolutely loved the moment when she defeated him from the kitchen. The open-source bit was also great, even if my lack of physics acumen meant I had absolutely no idea what they were talking about.  
 Not all the stories take place in a far future. Many weave together elements of contemporary life and Finnish mythology. "Fisher of Men" tells the story of an ambitious entrepreneur's run-in with Vellamo and Iku-Turso. "The Viper Blanket", which involves the myths of Tuoni, is a perfect blend of creepiness and mundanity. It starts with an old man checking his brother out of the nursing home as they discuss ritual sacrifice and then just keeps getting weirder from there. "The Oldest Game" weaves together one man's broken life and a contest with Pekko. 
 Some of the stories involve neither Finnish mythos nor possible futures. "Ghost Dogs" creates its own urban myth. It is a nostalgic, bittersweet story, told with a child's perspective and insight. "Paris, In Love," is a sentimental tale a Finnish man who falls in love with a city only to discover that the feeling is mutual. "Satan's Typist" is a disturbing bit of horror that puts a different perspective on hellish forms. 
 Several stories explore the way technology may shape humanity in the not-too-distant future. In "Topsight" ("The night before Kuovi was supposed to fly home, the four of them went to bring back Bibi's soul"), Kuovi finds her dead friend's "halo," a contraption of sensors with a brain-computing interface, and begins to wonder if it will let her see through Bibi's eyes. "The Jugaad Cathedral" ("On the day they finally got the Cathedral's mermaid bone factory working, Kev told Raija he was not going to come back.") explores not the threat of technology but of its regulation. It takes place in a future world where human interaction revolves around social networks, where every action and inaction is reflected in the numeric scores that describe each person's place in the world. Cloud computing is everywhere, but after the Lockdown, everything is monitored and regulated and limited and subject to DRM. "Shibuya no Love" ("They were eating takoyaki by the statue of Hachiko the dog when Norie told her to buy a quantum lovegety.") whimsically portrays a future in which artificial intelligence and advanced algorithms can predict far more than romantic compatibility. 
 Rajaniemi combines incredible technological expertise with such a vast imagination that many of his stories leave me overwhelmed by the worlds he creates. This collection demonstrates his breadth as well, involving everything from his invention of neurofiction to his stories of algorithmic romance to his tales that invoke ancient Finnish gods. Whatever the genre or subject, Rajaniemi's stories are guaranteed to be interesting, unique, and utterly captivating. If a science fiction author's job is to "think of impossible things," then I can't imagine anyone who does it better.

I loved this story. It would have been a favorite of mine when I was 10/9-11. 
 I finally got to it because of a recommendation from Izzy; I'm so glad that it didn't languish forever on my to read list, as do most of my "to read" books. 
 I loved August's voice so much that at first I was disappointed when another voice/several characters' voices started narrating the story. However, I ended up really appreciating the multiple perspectives. All of the kids' points of view are done perfectly, both the fifth graders and the ninth graders. 
 I had heard that there was one, and I could tell ahead of time what the sad animal moment would be, but at 10 I might not have seen it coming. 
 The story is very touching, and very funny, and very sweet. The ending was not my favorite, but that's okay; it worked well enough, and I appreciated why it ended the way it did. 
 I have some theories about one of the characters who wasn't given a voice, and I see that there is a published short story told from his point of view, but this book was so perfectly put together that I don't know that I have much interest in reading it. 
 I enjoyed seeing all the precepts included at the end of the book. 
 This is a great book about bullying, being kind, doing the right thing, being courageous, good teaching, friendship and family, and I respected how it didn't talk down to kids. I remember having these same kinds of deep conversations and thoughts when I was the age of Auggie and his classmates, and I think most readers around age 10 will identify with this group of kids. I also think that this could be a life-altering book for some young readers. And, it was simply a fun read and hard to put down. Very engaging.

In Requiem , Lauren Oliver's writing was great like usual and it was an overall enjoyable novel, although I do have mixed feelings about this novel. 
 Firstly, the book commences shortly after the end of Pandemonium . I was very intrigued with how Oliver would fabricate what would happen next. The focus was not only on the love triangle between Lena, Alex and Julian but also on how they cope throughout the novel, as well as the other characters as part of the resistance. 
 Structurally, the POV's switch between Lena and Hana which I found very interesting. Hana as a character for me develops substantially, and it was good to see what was happening on both sides of the fence. Unlike the other books before, Requiem was not as quickly paced like Pandemonium was, but Oliver does build it up gradually into the climax.  For instance, when Hana would count down the days to her wedding.  
 On the other hand, I don't know how I feel about the ending, there wasn't really a clear conclusion on what happened to the characters and the lack of closure annoyed me. In a way, it felt like the ending of the previous books. It felt like it ended on a cliffhanger. 
 I watched a video of Lauren Oliver explaining her reasons for ending the novel in such a way and I completely understand her point of view, in which having an ending like this allows us to interpret what would happen to the characters in the end. The lack of closure would also allow us to not fully feel as if we've left Lena's world as it's always sad to say goodbye to characters I've grown attached to. Alternatively, due to this I didn't feel as if this lived up to Delirium and Pandemonium because of how it ended. It would have been nice to atleast have an epilogue, but on the other hand, you can't deny that it's a beautiful book like the others. 
 Overall, I'd rate it 3.5 stars but rounded up to 4 on here. I absolutely adore this trilogy, I just didn't like Requiem as much as I wanted to.

Solid space opera, which came highly recced to me by my family -- including my sister, which was a surprise, because all SF is anathema to her. And it's a pretty good book -- a police procedural in spaaaace, the beginnings of a system-wide war, and some very likeable characters. The world building is excellent -- it's apparent that both authors had planned every part of the system with care and attention to detail; some of which cleverly plays into the scientific plausibility of the setting, like the use of large gestures that can be seen in spacesuits, spaceships designed like tower blocks (because drag isn't an issue) and the accounting for gs when travelling. 
 For me, the best part was the absolutely crazy ending. Eros careening across the solar system, and the macguffin finally getting a chance to produce something other than "vomit-zombies" was fascinating. I also really liked Miller as a character, and I'm sorry to see him go (? I'm assuming he's not coming back). The worst parts were the repetitive nature of some descriptions -- the first time a ship "became a sun" exploding in space was awesome, the third time it was tired -- and the lack of female characters who were anything other than a stereotype, or a "goal" for the male characters to achieve. It's not enough to make me think "ok, I won't read the next one", but I'd like a more balanced cast.

 Ahem. Anyway. There are a lot of ways in which I found this a very satisfying conclusion to the series. When I first heard about this author named David Levithan, I thought that he could possibly be the next (for me, anyway) John Green. You know, author of books about males with male problems with male feelings with male solutions. Yayayaya. As the years have gone by (it's really only been 18 months), I have found that Levithan (so far) has relatively disappointed me. 
 It's not that I don't like his subject matter, because that shouldn't really matter in the grand scheme of things. If one is a good author, their writing skills should supersede any mediocre plot. But um...David's writing just never does it for me, ever. 
 I've read three of his books so far, one of which was Dash & Lily's Book of Dares ( which was a joint effort; this is one of the only reasons why it was decent) and The Realm of Possibility (which I didn't even finish). I don't know. It straddles the line between angst and reflection and I know that sounds like a mildly good combination (especially a fan of Holden Caulfield such as myself) but when David does it, it sounds superfluous and bourgeois, as if he's writing a dissertation or something of that nature (aha. I hope you catch the irony in there) And in the case of this book, the plot was excellent but the writing...was slightly lacking. 
 Okay, let's get to the plot. There is this 'human' simply self-proclaimed 'A'. This person has the ability (or is cursed, which ever way you want to look at it) to travel from one body to another (within age range & geographic area constraint) each and every day (that's the title; did ya see what I did there? did ya?) A has never known another way of life. A has never had a real family (not including the ones he visits on any given day) and has trouble keeping friends or maintaining relationships for more than 24 hours. When A goes to sleep at night, A wakes up in a different body, be it male or female, white or black or asian or hispanic or whatever. It doesn't really matter. 
 But then A meets a girl named Rhiannon when A is placed into the body of her jerk of a boyfriend named Justin. A falls in love with her and unlike A has done with anyone, A pursues the relationship even as A travels through different bodies. A somehow expects Rhiannon to accept A's ...thing wholeheartedly and love A as much as A loves her. 
 Yeah. Okay. 
 This is a nice concept, yes? (Did I mention that A has no gender?) It's terrible to think about, to place yourself in A's shoes. A has to live a totally solitary life, living as hundreds of people all the time. And there is no reason placed behind this, it just IS and A has to deal with that. 
 Throughout the book, I found A a bit annoying. I mean, A wasn't too bad but enough for me to say, 'hey, shut up'. A was selfish (and I meant that in the best way possible) but I could understand why A did some of the things A did because, you know...his 'life' kinda sucks toe. I wasn't very fond of Rhiannon at all. Everything from her name to her complaining irritated me to no end. I never got the feeling that Rhinannon ever really reciprocated A's feelings and I don't blame her but I hated how A and Levithan pretended that she could. 
 Levithan is not shy about making social issue statements. Everything from suicide to drug use to homosexual couples is covered and (because they're teenagers) they are covered quite extensively. I just wish that I didn't feel like I was watching some kind of health video about teen issues. It was OKAY but...very odd and methodical. 
 I also didn't fancy the paragraphs used (but that's just a pet peeve of mine) and I abhorred how Levithan placed in these generic lines about love in there and I could just picture every last one of them lined up at the bottom of the book page under 'quotes'. Barf. It was so contrived and those lines could have been in any love book written in the last decade. 
 Anyway, this book wasn't all bad. It had a really nice cover and there were some parts I enjoyed. I wouldn't be all that interested in reading it again, just because it's so annoying the first time. I recommend it to...well I don't even know. I'm not sure I even recommend it, to be honest.

 A Week of Mondays by Jessica Brody 
 Publisher: Farrar, Straus and Giroux (BYR) 
 Publication Date: August 2, 2016 
 Rating: 4 stars 
 Source: ARC sent by the publisher 
 Summary (from Goodreads): 
 When I made the wish, I just wanted a do-over. Another chance to make things right. I never, in a million years, thought it might actually come true... 
 Sixteen-year-old Ellison Sparks is having a serious case of the Mondays. She gets a ticket for running a red light, she manages to take the world's worst school picture, she bombs softball try-outs and her class election speech (note to self: never trust a cheerleader when she swears there are no nuts in her bake-sale banana bread), and to top it all off, Tristan, her gorgeous rocker boyfriend suddenly dumps her. For no good reason! 
 As far as Mondays go, it doesn't get much worse than this. And Ellie is positive that if she could just do it all over again, she would get it right. So when she wakes up the next morning to find she's reliving the exact same day, she knows what she has to do: stop her boyfriend from breaking up with her. But it seems no matter how many do-overs she gets or how hard Ellie tries to repair her relationship, Tristan always seems bent set on ending it. Will Ellie ever figure out how to fix this broken day? Or will she be stuck in this nightmare of a Monday forever? 
 From the author 52 Reasons to Hate My Father and The Unremembered trilogy comes a hilarious and heartwarming story about second (and third and fourth and fifth) chances. Because sometimes it takes a whole week of Mondays to figure out what you really want. 
 What I Liked: 
 I've read one book by Brody - 52 Reasons To Hate My Father - and I really liked it. So I was looking forward to reading this new contemporary by Brody, especially when I saw that it had an interesting twist to it. Experiencing Monday over and over? That sucks! Until Ellie gets it right. 
 Ellie had a really bad Monday - she runs a red light, she forgets an umbrella, her election speech goes terribly, and her boyfriend breaks up with her. She just wants a do-over, and surprise! She wakes up the next day and it's still Monday. She does not realize it at first, but it becomes clear that she is stuck on Monday again, and it's just her that is experiencing this. But day after day, Monday after Monday, Ellie's boyfriend still breaks up with her. And the next day is still Monday. Will she be stuck experiencing this Monday, or will she get it right? 
 Brody definitely knows how to write a wonderful contemporary novel! Light and cute, this story was well-developed and intriguing, deceptively long though it read very quickly. I was eagerly turning pages, trying to figure out why Ellie kept experiencing her terrible Monday. 
 Ellie is a overachieving student, who is on the student government, will be on the softball team, has top grades and hard classes, and revels in her busy academic and social life. You can tell she's a dedicated student, as well as girlfriend. I liked Ellie a lot! She's in denial when Tristan breaks up with her, because he doesn't give a good reason as to why. As much as I didn't like Tristan, I liked how hard Ellie fought for her boyfriend. 
 Each Monday that Ellie experienced was very different from the first. The original, first Monday was awful. The second Monday was confusing. The Mondays after those were different, each crazier than the previous. Ellie grows a lot during and after each Monday. While this book takes place in just seven days, Ellie matures a great deal after each day. It's like she isn't allowed to go to Tuesday until she gets it right. 
 I already mentioned that I didn't like Tristan, and it's hard to like him. He's a secondary character, with a role that seems important to the story. But it's clear that he isn't as important as we think, because he doesn't have a ton of depth. The male character that DOES have good depth... 
 Owen. Owen is Ellie's best friend since middle school. Ellie picks him up in the morning to go to school every morning, which is where we see most of their interactions. Owen is the first and only person that Ellie tells about her repeating Monday situation. I liked him a lot - he's a little strange and quirky, but he's a perfect friend and a sweet guy. And (spoiler) a great love interest. 
 As we know from the synopsis, Tristan keeps breaking up with Ellie. But for the entire book, she's trying to get him to stay with her. But you can tell, as the book goes on, that she becomes less interested in Tristan and his antics. And she starts to realize that she has feelings for her best friend. I didn't see this as a love triangle, but that's subjective. 
 The ending is pretty great! I liked seeing Ellie's growth, in her academic life, her personal life, and her familial life. I especially like the romance in the end. But this contemporary novel had it all! Such a great story with positive relationships and a cute romance. 
 What I Did Not Like: 
 I wanted more Owen time and less I-need-to-stop-Tristan-from-breaking-up-with-me time. Not that what was written was bad! But I wanted more with Owen. Oweeeeen! 
 Would I Recommend It: 
 If you like cute contemporary, this is a great one! Jessica Brody seems to write some great stories, contemporary especially. I recommend this one, or 52 Reasons to Hate My Father! 
 Rating: 
 4 stars. This one was a long one, but a good one! It's as light and feel-good as you think it might be. I might not be in high school anymore, but I really connected with Ellie and her struggles, and I loved seeing her grow. Here's to Mondays! 
 Initial reactions, upon finishing the book: 
 I'll be posting my review on August 14th. But in the meantime, I'll write a few short thoughts. 
 I LOVED this book! There are seven parts, starting with the First Monday, and then Second Monday, Third Monday, all the way to the Seventh Monday. Ellie survives Monday, only to wake up the next day and realize that it's still Monday. She catches on after the Second Monday. She's very focused on using her second chances to make things right - with her boyfriend, who breaks up with her at the end of the First Monday. But it's not as easy as that - at the end of the next Monday, he still breaks up with her. So, what if keeping Tristan from breaking up with her isn't what she needs to make right? What if there is more to it? This book isn't solely focused on Ellie's relationship with Tristan - there is focus on Ellie's parents, Ellie and her sister, Ellie and her best friend Owen... I love how Brody crafts and develops characters, and relationships. There is NO love triangle in this book, but it depends on how you might see things. I don't see one. Tristan seemed too perfect and too focused on breaking up with Ellie.  I'm very happy with the romance although I wish there was more than one kissy scene, and I wish it wasn't JUST at the end. But then, I see why Brody only had the one kissy scene, and it was at the end. Anyway, I would totally recommend this book, especially to YA contemporary fans! I'm not a YA contemporary fan but I liked Brody's 52 Reasons to Hate My Father, and I knew this one would be very sweet and enjoyable and positive as well. And it was! 
 Full review to come on August 14th.

I nearly gave up on this book after the first 150 pages or so, since it seemed to be almost entirely a depiction of the minutiae of campus life in the 1970's so filled with dull and unnecessary detail that it seemed geared towards aliens who had never before heard of a "university" and had no idea what might go on in one. Most of the characters seemed personality-free and interchangeable, and even now I could not easily tell you the differences in character between Sharon and Molly and Nora and the dozen or so others whose names I forget because they all kind of sound the same. 
 I came even closer to tossing it aside after the next 100 pages, which consisted of characters who thought that quoting poetry made them deep having 101-level discussions about books and plays; that type of discussion can definitely be fun and rewarding to participate in but, as it turns out, it is some kind of personal version of hell to read about other people having them, at least for me. Meanwhile, a number of plays that the characters saw were recounted in their entirety for some reason. It turns out there is little less exciting than reading about other people watching something, even when they laugh uproariously at jokes that aren't shared with the reader, which happens frequently. 
 Throughout all this, some obviously supernatural events are occasionally occurring, which both the characters and the narrative largely ignore to focus on the poem-quoting, play-watching, class-scheduling, etc. While there was an in-book reason for these events to be ignored, the result was not exactly a plot that rockets along propulsively. 
 To be fair, the back half of the book picks up considerably. The book starts acknowledging that, up until that point, the characters have been acting like the shallow, immature college freshmen they were, which makes the main character's flaws seem much more forgivable; some of the characters start seriously dating which finally leads to a bit of forward plot movement and results in the literary analysis actually having some bearing on the situation for once; the main character decides that the bizarrely supernatural events going on are worthy of at least some investigation. This is never going to be a favorite book, but at least when it ended I didn't feel that I'd completely wasted my time. However, the first half was such a slog that I can't give it more than two stars. 
 Honestly, I would recommend starting this book somewhere around chapter 13 to 15. Sure, you'll feel lost and won't know who anyone is, but you'll have missed surprisingly little plot or character development, and you'll be reading a much better book than the whole thing uncut.

 1. That humans judge God by their own standards 
 2. That Jesus died to forgive our sins and therefore we don't need to be bound by legalism; doing so is just another way of asserting our own righteousness/authority. 
 3. The Trinity. The author seems to have a decent understanding of it and attempts to explain it, aware of the inherent limitations in our understanding of it. 
 In the "miss" section goes the authors beliefs (or at least points) about salvation. It basically seemed like he was advocating universal salvation, even though he seemed to pretend not to be. Also I feel like putting words in the mouth of God/Jesus is a slippery slope.

 I also wasn't clear if the "framing it as a true story" was a literary device or if someone claims this actually happened to him. Guess I should Wikipedia it. 
 I feel the merit of this book for me was largely to take a look at my own beliefs as contrasted with the author's. I certainly wouldn't recommend it as a way to learn about faith or anything like that. If you're curious, it's a quick read (3 hours for me) but it's not a must-read by any stretch.
