 I would probably give this book 2.5 stars if I could, but I was definitely more on the "it was ok" side of the ratings than the "liked it" side. 
 The thing that I really liked about this book was the writing. Adam Rex really captured the kind of teen banter and lingo that I think so many YA novelists just totally miss. It's probably one reason why I don't read as much "realistic" YA fiction as I read the fantasy kind. I just can't stand the cliche dialogue, the eye-rolling "god Moms," and the I'm-so-full-of-angst-and-I-play-video-games-and-talk-on-my-cell-phone-cause-I'm-a-teen-and-that's-what-we're-all-like-these-days stock characters. Give me a Harry Potter-esque, hero in the rough over that any day. But Adam Rex's teen dialogue, refreshingly, did not fall into this trap. It was funny (I think I actually lol-ed a few times) and it felt real. The character's voices felt legitimate. At times, I caught myself remember when I actually felt just like that, just what Rex was describing, in high school. 
 What I didn't like about this book was the story. It started off great (what a great prologue!), and just kind of...didn't go anywhere. It was as if Rex created these characters with all this potential for an interesting, not-your-usual-teen-vampire-story but then left them on the page while he made a sandwich. And they just kind of....wandered around for a while, doing this and that, killing time but never doing anything. I think I kind of get it, what he was trying to "say". Doug is supposed to be a non-hero, a "normal" guy (which I guess his fatness implies??), who just happens to have been turned into a vampire. His crush says to him in the prologue something like, "you're always assuming you're either the villain or the hero in your story when actually you're neither." And I think that pretty much sums up Doug and Fat Vampire. But the problem whith a "normal" main character is that they can be boring. And it's like Doug's normalness infects the rest of the book. So even though a couple of creepy, vampire-y things do eventually happen to Doug in this book, I found myself asking, "who cares?" 
 And the ending.... don't even get me started on the ending. It turned into something like a "choose your own adventure" throwback. Does Doug die a horrible bloody death or does he survive to become a totally average and bitter man: you decide! Again, I get it. It doesn't matter what happened to Doug because he's emphatically not the hero of this story. But, he's still the main character (the book is named after him after all), and we are currently reading a normal, conventional novel. I think it's way too jarring to insert that kind of meta-textual stuff at the very end of the story out of nowhere. Or, go ahead and insert it, but then give us an "actual" ending that we can latch on to rather than just kind of not...ending it...

Molly is a foster kid that has been shipped around numerous times since her father's death. With only a 3 charm necklace keepsake, Molly has little comfort. When she steals an old copy of Jane Eyre from the library, Molly compromises with her boyfriend to do her community service cleaning 91-year-old Vivian's attic. The task seems unbearable at first until Vivian slowly opens up to Molly about her own heroine ordeals. 
 Vivian is an elderly woman, living in the comfort of a large mansion by the sea. Having been orphan after an apartment fire that had claim her family, Vivian (Niamh, her birth name) ends up on the cross country orphan train. Each item in Vivian's attic symbolizes her past: a mustard coat from her time with the seamstress, an old copy of Anne and the Green Gables from her time in a broken down shack, a tea set from her time in a boarding house for young ladies. Vivian connects to the young foster child through her own memories and each of them heal the other's wounds. 
 I really like the story of the Orphan Train. I never heard of this event, ever, until I picked this book up. Kline's writing is like a young adult book without the problems of young adult. The research that went into this book, and the description of all kinds of children. A majority of the book takes place in Minnesota (for Vivian) and Maine (for Molly). Vivian's portions were my favorite parts of the book. Her inner dialog did not bored me as with so many historical fiction novels. The writing of a child that spends most of her life not expecting to be care of, is absolutely heartbreaking. 
 Vivian feels like a real character for me. Molly does too, but Molly doesn't impact me as much as Vivian did. Vivian's talk about her Irish history, and Molly's talk about her Indian history are what makes Orphan Train the book it is. Two different people, cultures with a common problem: being told to hide who they truly are. 
 I would recommend this book to people that love historical fiction, female characters, and a fast pace read. However, it is best to keep an open mind that even though Vivian and Molly's situations are realistic, that a majority of foster homes are loving and caring places.

ARC provided by Give Me Books Promotions. 
 B is Jenna's best friend, the third wheel in her relationship with Jamie, the one that is there for both of them and the one that will be there for them years down the road when everything is different. Except Jamie is more like an intoxicating whiskey than man, it's impossible to not crave him, and he's back on her door step after a year, just like he has been all the years before. Over the course of a decade they fight the addiction they share, neither strong enough to resist the taste. 
 I would never admit it, but even then, I was already itching for another taste. 
 A Love Letter to Whiskey is one of those books that you will tell all your friends about, that you'll push them to read, that you'll exclaim about how relatable it is. Because that's exactly what it is, relatable, in an agonizing way that makes your heart break. It resembles life and how people are so perfectly. It's a hard read, the kind that might be too emotional for some, but it's absolutely worth all the feelings. B, the protagonist, will make you angry, she'll have you wanting to toss the book to the side, but she'll also have you looking at yourself, your relationships, and life around you. Over the course of a decade you grow to love B, and sometimes hate her too, as she grows independent, as she falls in and out of love, as she discovers who she is and who Jamie really is to her. Jamie was immediately a favorite for me, it's hard not to love the guy that's such a good friend even when he wants so much more. I can't say I liked everything he did, but goodness I loved his dedication. These two share a complicated history, a decade long love story that hurts to read let alone experience, but you root for them all the same. 
 I always loved that, the first sight of him, the first hit. It was a little jarring, like a slight burn, but the aftertaste was smooth, welcoming, like an old friend calling me home. 
 Kandi Steiner's writing is incredible in A Love Letter to Whiskey, I never expected all of the emotions she elicited from me. I adored the lyrical writing and how Kandi pulled the reader into the past, bringing us along to ride the roller coaster with B. I wanted a drink just as bad as B pined for her shot of Whiskey and I found myself highlighting more passages than I can count. It's a complex story of friendship, of making choices, and learning how to overcome fears. I at first hated the idea of comparing two people's connection to one another to an alcohol addiction, but goodness how true it was for these two. Their addiction was all consuming and I felt like I was coming down with them as I rode the highs and lows. Like real life, this book is all about timing and how impossible it is to make time be on your side. 
 I believed him when he said that, but sometimes we say things we don't mean. We may mean them in the moment the words leave our lips, but as time goes on, good intentions get rubbed raw by failed expectations. Those on the promising end forget why they promised at all, hearts jaded - for good reason. 
 I know a lot of people who hate emotional reads, who shy away from ugly-cry novels, who want nothing to do with a realistic story line, but this book is worth every single angry or hurt or elated emotion you feel while reading. I couldn't walk away from it, staying up well past my bedtime, because I couldn't quit with these two characters and their epic love story. The prose is beautiful and the story gripping, A Love Letter to Whiskey is the kind of book that belongs on the best seller list. I think every reader should get drunk on Kandi's words, I know I did, and I won't be the same now that I've met B and Jamie. 
 He couldn't have known how those words would sit with me. He couldn't have known that they'd snake their way in-between the bones of my rib cage, winding tight, cutting of my ability to breathe with their truth.

Sarina is living the dream. She has a successful business as an architect, a stable, well-off boyfriend, and the best friends that anyone could ever ask for. Everything is going the way she had planned until Eamon Roy shows up in Austin. Eamon Roy, the only one night stand Sarina ever had. Eamon, Roy, Olympic swimmer. Eamon Roy, her new architectural client. With Eamon's home renovation project, she'll be seeing much more of him than she had anticipated and with her boyfriend off to Argentina for the year, she isn't sure how much she can take. 
 This is a pretty strong debut from Bethany Chase. I loved Sarina's voice. She sounded real to me in a way that many romance novel heroines don't. Her quirky sense of humor and quick wit made her light up for me and really got me rooting for her. Eamon was swoon worthy and their chemistry was dynamite. Noah, on the other hand, seemed like a contemptible twit the whole story - I wish there had been a little more of him at the start, to give the reader the feel of him as a round character, rather than one squashed by work and a long distance relationship. The pacing of the story seemed a little slow at times, but never slow enough that I put the book down and walked away. I appreciated the reality of complex relationships. A break-up is never cut and dried; the start of a relationship is sometimes fraught with miscommunication and jealousy. Even though there are some tough moments, this is, for the most part, a pretty fluffy read. Readers of Jennifer Weiner, Susan Elizabeth Phillips, and Jennifer Cruise will enjoy. I most certainly am looking forward to her next book.

A very funny book. This autobiography had several places where I found myself laughing out loud. I read Lawson's second book, Furiously Happy first, and that was quite good, but this one is even better. Highly recommended.

After Legend, I needed more. I couldn't wait for Prodigy. Marie Lu always leaves you wanting more after you finish one of her novels, and that's what I'm feeling right now. I need Champion, ASAP. 
 Prodigy was really good. The beginning just left off where Legend did, and the events and unstoppable things that happened just made me want to squeal. I am a total fangirl for this series, and couldn't have asked for a better middle to the trilogy... okay maybe one that was a little better. I felt that the story wasn't as strong as the first book, but never mind, it was really good. 
 I loved the sneakiness that Day and June did together, they're a squad, they're a team, they're a couple, and I love them. June is superb, and is a strong woman, but when her memories come back to her, the overtake her, and completely change her. Day is adorable, and is definitely the mastermind behind everything the couple does. 
 Great and heart-stopping.

I loved this sweet Cinderella story and every character in it--Uptight Morgan, Caustic Isabel, Romantic Norman, and Damaged Colie. And then Mira, obese, artistic, colorful, whimsical, wise....Mira was the mentor for them all. 
 Dessen is an obvious master at crafting flaws, inner turmoil, and realistic, lovely relationships. How refreshing to see a friendship (and one between a set of secondary characters, no less) be the focal point of this story-- an "I love you despite your flaws" friendship. An "I'll tell you the truth even if it hurts" friendship. An "I'll go down swingin' to defend you" friendship. Isabel and Morgan's was an incredible love story; pitch-perfect and beautiful. I'd love to see another novel written about them in middle age--or even as seniors--because the way they were together? 
 That's how women are supposed to treat each other. 
 And the theme here is also such a refreshing take on the age-old problem of bullying; Dessen employs the "other people's opinion of you is none of your business" adage and oh, indeed. Mira couldn't give a flying fig what all the Filthy McNasties in her little town have to say. She merely rides her bike (with a bell!), pastes her loud clothing all over her way-large person and gobbles all the high-sugar cereal she can get her mitts on. If she notices anyone's snark she most certainly ignores it and, in her house full of broken possessions, and amid her greeting card art and passion for wrestling, Mira is not only content but deeply happy. She's a hero, and the way she chooses to live is a new way of taking the wind from the sails of a tired old tyranny done time and again: Mean Girls and the cruelty they wreak. 
 Screw 'em, says Mira, by ignoring them completely. You go, girl. 
 The tiniest criticism (that doesn't erase any stars) is Kiki Sparks. She might be a fitness and weight loss mogul, but she's the world's crappiest parent who's never called out for such and, amongst all the other characters whose feet are held to the fire for the mistakes they make, Kiki being revered by both Mira and Colie stuck out for me like a sore thumb. Booo, Kiki. Mira is a thousand times the woman you are--in every way. 
 Kiki aside, I adored this sweet story and plowed through it in no time. 5 Happy Stars for one of the best pieces of chick-lit I've read in ages, and a bonus Star for this new discovery (for me) of the wonderful Sarah Dessen

Review originally posted on my blog: A Book Obsession.. 
 I don't typically read anthologies unless they are set in worlds that I already read, but I decided to give this one a shot. I'm really glad I did as I have a new series to read, and two of my favorite series have been expanded upon. Definitely a great read for fans of these series, or anyone looking for something new to try out. 
 Onto the stories: 
 Secrets at Midnight by Nalini Singh - I'm a huge fan of Nalini's archangel series, but I haven't read anything from her psy series. If this novella is any comparison to the rest of the series, then it seems I have been missing out. Boy is it hot! That being said, I don't think this was really the best place for a new comer to start in the series, because I was more than a little lost as to the world and what was going on outside of the main couple. Even so, an enjoyable read that makes me want to check out the full books. 
 Magic Steals by Ilona Andrews - THIS novella is the entire reason I wanted to read this anthology. I've been dying to see Jim and Dali's story since their attraction had been first hinted about a couple of books ago in the series. I absolutely loved seeing them together, and Dali is a really interesting character to see inside her head. Now I wish there was going to be a full length from her perspective. Even so, I'm really happy I got to read this story, and see another side to the mysterious Jim. 
 The Beast of Blackmoor by Milla Vane - This one was a difficult read for me. I just don't think barbarian stories are my thing as I couldn't really get into it. Don't get me wrong, it was sexy, but it was a bit too out there for my tastes. 
 Lucky Charms by Lisa Shearin - I have to admit that I completely spaced on what this story was until I started it. I absolutely loved the first book in this series, so it was really great to see this prequel story. Now I just can't wait to get my hands on book two as this fun story reminded me just how fun the book was, and how much I loved it. If you're looking for a new urban fantasy read, these are the ones to check out, lots of fun!
Stephanie Plum, inept bounty hunter. Very funny reads. They are kinda like Pringles... You can't just read one.

Three stars because 1) It's not YA - but not totally for adults either 2) The story was interesting and entertaining, and I didn't want to put the book down 
 BUT (some spoilers) 
 Worldbuilding: 
 I don't want to hear about wolves as a symbol again (I love wolves, the animal) in a Fantasy world. It's overdone. Take bears, lynxes, rabbits... anything else. 
 I like to read about mountains, snow, castles but there must be more to it: Make us feel the hunger. Give something scary. Describe the tunnels. What was in there? Then what with the food? If not everyone gets some from the start, most of their time should be invested in hunting (which is not that easy. And hunt several wolves? With spears? haha). What with the sea and Neptune House? I understand they get help for material and food but it feels like everything appears out of nowhere. The not enough "show don't tell" doesn't help. 
 The story: 
 It was more than promising during the Passage. You feel the hard choices. You suffer for Julian. The events in House Mars escalate and keep the suspense alive. Then it turns previsible, they all look the same (no character development, Darrow is perfect in everything...), and the end is rushed and botched. (Aaaand the classic: "I'm not going to kill the bad guy. I want to make a speech first and be loyal and wait until he butchers all my friends") Mustang: What a *surprising* twist. Will he succeed? There's two more books so you know he's going to make it. 
 I can't believe the Gold want to sacrifice so many of their children. I can understand (in their logic) that they want to get rid of the disappointing 50% (Yet, if they can't refuse the invitation and Julian's dad is genuinely sad, why don't some of them protest against the system? Priam's death shows that there are major flaws) but the children that are left just strive to stay alive. They are no heroes, no leaders... At least, Sparta sent their children alone in the wilderness and each one could prove his worth. Here, if you're not the Primus or his close followers, you're a pawn. Where is the family pride in that? 
 Darrow went through all this and he still sees the Gold as an homogenous class, he still wants to butcher all and everyone with his army of Reds (all so good and righteous Reds - because a Red rapist will always be a better brother than a nice Gold. Ugh). He's learned nothing. *Sigh* 
 The message: 
 There was nothing new here. The rich, the poor, the lower class... Though this message has been delivered again and again by classics (1984, The Running Man) and the mainstream Hunger Games/Divergent, people keep behaving like *pixies*. Let's face it. It doesn't work. Time to come with a book about solutions now. Or maybe too many stopped reading books?

This is a very cute YA fantasy novel about a princess who is sent to another court under semi-competition circumstances to get to know the prince who is looking for marriage prospects. 
 A major theme of this novel is making friends and fitting in with the popular crowd without sacrificing values (friendship,loyalty, basic niceness, etc.) and our heroine does this very well. SS also does a nice job of giving complex motivations even to her nasty characters. 
 The whole thing though is a bit like the high school prom moved to a magical realm with princes and princesses. As such it is sweet and uncomplicated and relatively satisfying without being especially deep. 
 I did think the action sequences were somewhat rushed and implausible. But this was made up for with the princess' interactions with her beau. Although I saw the twist coming for miles and I had a problem with  the long distance relationship at the end. 5 years only writing once a year? That's moving from the realm of plausible impossibility to impossible plausibility, or whatever that means... but I didn't completely want to buy it.  . Nevertheless, I recommend this book for anyone looking for a nice, light YA fantasy. 
 (And I was very happy that finally we got a SS character where a huge fricken deal wasn't made about her ass-length hair. What's the deal with that anyway? Although I love the cleaning frames and waste spells that are a feature of this universe. Magically getting rid of dirt and all uhm bodily discharges -- that's awesome.)

I first read this in high school and didn't remember much about it other than liking it. I recently listened to the audiobook version read by Maggie Gyllenhaal. This is a powerful story of a woman's struggles with mental illness perhaps enhanced by the conformity of the 1950s. I was particularly struck by Esther's attitudes toward sex and marriage. Maggie Gyllenhaal did an excellent job of narrating the novel and this would make a good discussion title for groups interested in reading classics.

An excellent work by an author who, despite the blurb, has been able to write a fantasy novel that breaks out of the 'Game of Thrones meet X' formula. For all the influence of Chinese culture on the book, there are also distinct nods to Japanese and Polynesian culture, and, on top of that, Liu has made Dara in to a setting that rises above its influences and becomes its own distinct world. 'Silkpunk' may be an appropriate way to describe this setting, though I somewhat flinch at calling it that nonetheless. 
 For all the strength of the setting, the big draw for me were the strong characters and humanism that drives Liu's writing. Kuni was by far the most entertaining character, and it's quite fun to watch his rise from common layabout to, well, I won't spoil anything. Sometimes he verges in to Mary Sue territory, he seems to be the guy that knows everything, likes everyone, and always makes the best decision possible. Even immortal magic whales seem to think he's amazing. Despite this, Kuni is still Kuni and not simply a bland superman. Mata, the story's other protagonist (slash antagonist), IS a bland superman though, which is exactly the point, and as much as I loved Kuni and hated Mata, I ended up thinking he was by far the more interesting character. 
 Mata is a little weird, btw, eight feet tall with oft-commented on double-pupils. I have no idea where the pupil thing comes from, but it was a little weird and kind of threw me off, especially since it's never clear why he has these odd features. Anyway, Mata struck me as very much an emotionally stunted man-baby, born for war and good at literally nothing else. In every way that Kuni succeeds he fails, fails to act appropriately, fails to see reason, fails to adapt. In some way he was a bit one-dimensional (whereas Kuni certainly has dimensions to spare), but it was never hard to understand why he was the way he was, nor was it hard to believe people like him exist. 
 The ancillary characters were all excellent, too many to mention and memorable to the last one, with the possible exception of Kuni's magic second wife, who was enigmatic and didn't seem to have much to do beyond trotting out her smoke-based powers and feeling uncomfortable around his first wife, who was great. Gin Mazoti,as many have commented, was the best character in the book. Not only Liu's nod to proto-feminism in this world grappling with modern ideas, she was also fairly well-rounded and, well, a badass 
 The power of technology to affect social change is an important theme in the book, and throughout we are exposed to technology that seems both fanciful and surprisingly well thought out. Dara seems to be going through an industrial revolution of sorts, possessing technology that is, in some cases, formidable for all time. If you haven't heard by now, there are airships, and they rock. Lots of other interesting innovations come in to play in the story, both in expected and unexpected way. Though for the most part very fun and giving the story a unique flavor, it does contribute to my annoyance at Kuni and his cadre of super-visionaries. Kuni always sees the wisdom in every forward-thinking idea imaginable, and they always bear fruit towards a better future, with minimal unintended consequences. This can even extend to thing like tax codes, which are never explained in detail, but, we are assured, are eminently reasonable. Liu, bucking the somewhat overhyped trend in fantasy towards grimdark, is an uninhibited idealist (though not, in my mind, an unrealistic one) and this can explain his character's habit of rolling all sixes when it come to technological innovation and social progress. We all know this is not how it works though, and I wished I could have seen more of the failures, upheavals, and regressions that typically come with progress. 
 Lots of this kvetching makes it sounds like I didn't love this book, rest assured, I did, and I stand firm in giving it five stars. Grace of Kings is, above all, lots of fun, and filled with thoughtful and provocative insights in the tradition of the best fantasy lit. I am quite interested to see where the story is going to go, since it is already listed as 'Book #1', and although the ending resolved quite a bit, there were certainly some loose threads left hanging. We shall see. On an added note, anyone who liked Grace of Kings should certainly check out Daniel Abraham's Long Price Quartet, which has some indisputable similarities (Asian milieu, rising technology, blue collar protagonist that come up big) and is every bit as good.

I enjoyed this book and learning about Moloka'i, but found it difficult to read because it was so sad. The story follows Rachel through her life, from her childhood to when she's taken from her home after contracting leprosy to the life she builds for herself on Moloka'i. I liked that through Rachel and the people she meets, you learn the full history of Moloka'i, not just the timeframe that Rachel lives there. The setting was beautifully described and I felt like I was able to really visualize Hawaii. My only real criticism is that I didn't feel that connected to Rachel, or any of the characters in this novel. I recommend this book, but with the warning that at times it's hard to read because it's so sad.

Solid but a bit boring at times. The world seemed interesting enough but it lacked something that I can't put my finger on. It was an enjoyable read but the characters were a bit thin and I don't think I'll be reading any of the following books unless it somehow grows on me, which I don't foresee happening. Don't get me wrong, it wasn't a terrible story and I certainly enjoyed it well enough but there wasn't much in there to compel me to come back to this world.
This is about so much more than it says and it took me by surprise in the best way.

I just love the covers of these books. Wow, I didn't expect all that to happen. Rachel Vincent keeps you guessing. Some of the story was a bit predictable but a lot of it I had no clue about. This series is getting good. I wonder what is in store next for Kaylee?

Honestly, not my type of book. I'm more a young adult, paranormal, romance fan, although I do enjoy Jodi Picoult. The Help however just wasn't my cup of tea, so I won't take it to heart if you blow off my review. I can see how it became a bestseller and now has a movie deal. The imagery in this novel was powerful but I was bored through most of the book. 
 Skeeter needed to just woman up and take ownership of her unconventional thoughts and actions. For the times, she was well more advanced than Hilly and the other girls. She needed to take some lessons from Minny, because she definitely was my favorite character. Could definitely have left out the Awful, terrible incident because OMG that really is disgusting. I felt for Aibleen more than the others, she just had this way with her. It's very hard to explain. 
 So this wasn't a terrible read, but it wasn't that great either. Won't be checking out the movie.

I was pleasantly surprised by this book. So many people compared it to Fifty Shades of Grey, which I loved by the way, but I was hesitant that the storyline would be too emotionally wrenching. Sometimes I get too caught up in stories and it can be overwhelming to be right there with the characters when they're experiencing tough emotions. When I read that this book was about two abuse survivors, all I could think about was a codependency drama disaster that was going to violate my mind in uncomfortable ways. I'm happy to say though that I'm glad I took a chance on this one, it was worth the read and this book was able to take me through a comfortable range of emotions without taking me to dark places. 
 While there were some major differences, I can definitely see why the Fifty Shades comparison. However, while I really really liked this book (it's much more grounded in my opinion than 50) I still think the story and blazing attraction between Christian and Ana spoke more directly to me. That's not to say this book can't hold it's own though. Sylvia Day is a much better writer than EL James and had Fifty Shades been written with her experience I believe that it would have surpassed much of the criticism that it has received. 
 Bared to You was a refreshing read. Eva is a woman who has a real depth to her emotions, not the cardboard cutouts that have become so popular with protags such as Bella and Ana. The way Eva feels and responds to Gideon is intense but it's not intense in a vacuous way. Eva has a dark past and it shows through in the way that she acts and responds to other people, Gideon in particular. I felt through the entire book that her emotions were justified because we as readers had something to base them on. There was none of that crap about characters getting pissed and storming off leaving the reader wondering what the hell they're so upset about. With Eva, you know exactly where she's coming from. She has a great deal of personal insight and her inner dialogue is very insightful and mature, no doubt due to her many years of therapy. She is a well developed character and it shows. This really gave a deeper layer and a sense of reality to the story. Of course Gideon and Cary are also great characters. (I just didn't find myself swooning over Gideon like I did for Christian though). They all meld together in an enticing way and it's easy to see how and why they fit together. 
 Seeing as how this probably also classifies as erotica, it bears mentioning that the sexual tension (and easement) between Eva and Gideon is just as gratifying as it was between Christian and Ana in Fifty Shades of Grey and the emotional connection (from reader to story) was even better. I'm looking forward to reading more about Eva and Gideon.

This was enjoyable, but not perfect. The story of Naomi, a girl who is in love with her gay best friend, and Eli-the gay best friend that just doesn't get it. Things finally boil over when Eli steals Naomi's (formerly straight) boyfriend. It is time for both characters to grow up and move on, which over the course of the book they do. However, this story is told in alternating first person chapters--narrated by a variety of characters, some of whom only have one chapter in the whole book. It makes the whole thing seem slightly disjointed, and I would even occasionally be confused as to who the character was. Not as good as Dash and Lilly's book of Dares, but still worth a read.

5+++ stars for The Mistress! This is an incredibly rich and completely satisfying conclusion to the Original Sinners series. All of the characters are brought together in The Mistress and their rich and complex stories are told in a very clever and gripping way. I can't do justice to a book that is so masterfully written and so filled with erotic and sensual images that I literally could not put it down. 
 You must read The Original Sinners series first so that you will be familiar with the intricate and complex histories of the gorgeous and fierce characters created by Tiffany Reisz. In The Mistress, Nora is forced to recount stories of her past with Kingsley and Soren. 
 "You're my favorite monster, she said against his lips." 
 "She felt pleasure with other men, ecstasy even sometimes...but only when Soren was inside her did she feel whole. 
 Soren and Kingsley spring into action to rescue Nora and both recall their memories of their relationship with Nora and with each other." 
 "Soren could not live in a world without Nora. Kingsley could not live in a world without Soren." 
 Wesley also rushes to help rescue Nora, along with Zachary's wife, Grace. Soren's niece Laila also forms an important part of the author's elaborate story of love, submission and erotica, a story that does not contain one false move or one unimportant character. 
 I don't want to give away any spoilers but suffice it to say that Tiffany Reisz has created a brilliant cast of characters and a story that will challenge you, thrill you and leave you breathless with anticipation. I was on the edge of my seat while reading The Mistress, hoping that Soren and Nora's unbreakable bond would get then through this latest crisis. 
 "The fire of her teenage infatuation with Soren had burned itself out years ago. In its flames a love made of iron had been forged. It could survive any blow, any trial." 
 The ending of this story was incredibly emotionally satisfying, and perfect for each character. The Mistress is a brilliant ending to an absolutely amazing series. 
 5+++ stars 
 Thanks to Harlequin and NetGalley for an ARC in exchange for an honest review.

This is the first time I've ever read anything like this. I've never been a huge comic fan so I didn't really have any expectations, I just knew I needed to read one to tick a box for a challenge and this seemed to be appearing on my feed a lot. 
 I actually ended up really enjoying this entertaining and quick read. There are moments of pure hilarity and I loved how sassy Nimona was as a character. I also liked how the themes of hero/villain were approached in the story, breaking from the more traditional approach. There were also plenty of sad moments and I enjoyed reading a little about Nimona's background. 
 I thought the illustrations were excellent and I liked the use of colour to represent different locations and stages in time. I thought this was a really well written and creative piece that I found myself really enjoying, despite it being outside of my normal comfort zone.

This quick read gives a new take on the Cinderella story by casting Ella, a spunk girl who was given the "gift" of obedience at birth, into the role of the abused stepsister. There have been TONS of retellings of fairy tales in recent years, so this story definitely felt less fresh for me than it probably would have when it first came out in 1997. Nonetheless, it was funny at times, and Ella is a realistically rebellious teenage girl. I would definitely recommend this book to girls who enjoy tales of princesses and fairy tales, especially those who are just transitioning into longer chapter books from beginning readers or Magic Treehouse type books. If they like this, I would be sure to check out Princess Academy by Shannon Hale for a similar princess story with an equally spunky heroine.

I can see why Stephen King likes this so much; he found someone who hates editors as much as he does. 
 This story is much better appreciated if you understand and accept that it was written as a serial. Also, if you accept this was written in Victorian times so you have to let your dirty mind fill in all the dirty bits. I think there's a lot of dirty parts, although I can't understand how seeing a girl have sex with a satyr would break a pubescent boy's mind so effectively that he became an invalid for the remainder of his life.
one of the best stories ever!!! the twist of mythology, the intriguing plot! i just wanted to read more and more!!!! i love this book, its great!

3.5 stars 
 Tracker's End was...one helluva lot of fun. Sexy, funny, awesome heroine, a pierced cock and some Ed Sheeran fandom happening. I had a good time as Tracker and Lana finally did something about their year long attraction and the 'good girl' snagged herself a biker. 
 I loved the heroine of this one. Lana was fantastic. A spot geeky, a bit inexperienced but not naive, a romance writer and just a likable woman with a good heart that would be easy to be around. 
 Tracker was pretty damn hot too. Sexy and cocky and rocking some hardware on his manly bits. I freaking LOVE pierced cocks so was all woohoo! over that. He could be an ass, could be incredibly sweet and could really fuck things up. 
 Heat-wise. These two pretty damn hot. Lots of passion and tension and a heroine that made him wait until they'd gotten to know each other a bit before having sex--yes for an awesome heroine once again. I do wish more had been done with the pierced cock which other than mentions there at the start was mostly ignored. But that's okay, I knew it was there. I liked these two together in and out of bed. They had very different personalities but they meshed well and brought out new and fun sides to each other. She got a little bold and sassy and adventurous--living life instead of just writing about it. And she softened his hard edges. Calmed and centered him. 
 I did have one issue that was a fairly big one and that was the hero's screw up. He pulled a Ross Geller and a 'we were on a break' bit and even though I enjoyed the book, the romance and how things ended I was pretty damn disappointed in him even at the close of the book.  He got pissed at her over a scene she was writing for her book, kicked her out without letting her explain then proceeded to get a blow job from some skank. He had a cheatery past with his ex as well and I had a hard time after that really believing he could stay faithful. He really didn't grovel enough or prove himself after that either. At least not enough for me. She didn't take him right back--again yay for the heroine--but I did think he got off way too easy on that front.  
 Now. On the MC front. On a scale of 1 to Madeline Sheehan...Tracker's End is a one when it comes to being an MC romance.  The basis of the story is basically x-men. Which is widely talked about. But honestly, even though I love x-men, if I hadn't heard that, I might have not made the connection. The setting and story is so different that it works. 
 There are reds, and there are silvers. Silvers (who have silver blood) are the elite class of royalty that have god-like powers. Super strength, telepathy, controllers of elements, etc etc. Reds (red blood) do not. Except Mare. She has a unique ability that causes quite at stir. The King and Queen declare her as a long lost Silver to hide the truth about her blood, all the while, she is secretly aiding a revolution. 
 There is a lot of action and a bit of romance but it is believable. It's by far insta-love. Character development is a little on the bland side. They don't have the greatest depth, but I've come to accept that in YA. My heart didn't pour out in feelings for the main character, but did more-so for some of the supporting characters. Julian, ah I loved him. I would have loved more backstory on him. He's a character with a story all his own that I would love to read. 
 Cal and Maven, the two princes, I constantly flip flopped on. I loved Cal, then Maven, then I loathed Cal, then Maven. Ugh. It was good though, I liked that I was constantly changing how I felt about them. It kept things fresh. 
 Evangeline can piss off. She wasn't that strong of an antagonist to Mare, not as bad as the Queen was. I can see why the author added her in but I didn't seethe hatred towards her like I did the Queen. 
 I really wished there was more of Kilorn and Farely. They really sounded at the beginning like important characters but it went a while before they were mentioned again. I would have loved to have seen an alternating pov to the side of the Scarlet Guard. There wasn't really a reason to not know what was going on from their side. 
 My overall feeling of this book was that it is definitely solid, an easy read, but (and I do this with all ya, dystopian or not) it fell short in comparison to The Hunger Games. It was great, I'm glad I read it and will be picking up Glass Sword, but I did not get that same sense of despair and longing for more like I did after hunger games.  The concept of the Wallflowers is centered around 4 young ladies in London who are, well, wallflowers, and they are each in need of a good husband. 
 This book is centered around Annabelle Peyton. Probably one of the prettiest of the wallflowers, she is a lady of society but her family has fallen down on their luck after the death of her father. It seems very appropriate to post my review of the Fug Girls' most recent book (their baby, so to speak) on the same day that the Duchess of Cambridge gave birth to her second baby. 
 This book starts the night before American Rebecca Porter is about to marry the heir to the British throne, as she's trying not to freak out about the fact that she's being blackmailed and her twin sister isn't speaking to her at all. 
 Cut to many years previous, when she arrives in Oxford in the rain, and the handsome young man who opens the door for her and helps her with the luggage turns out to be none other than Prince Nicholas, eldest grandson to Queen Eleanor and heir to the throne of Great Britain. Unlike her twin sister, Lacey, who used to dress up as a Disney princess and who obsessively reads gossip magazines for royal gossip, Bex (oh dear Lord how I hate that nickname) was never all that concerned, and despite sharing a corridor with Nick (or Steve as he is called when supposed to be incognito) doesn't impact her life overmuch in the beginning. She does realise that with the exception of his loyal inner circle of friends, most people are trying to gain something from their association wit the prince and his loyal friends frequently plant fake stories with different people just to see who can't be trusted not to blab to the press. 
 When Night Nick (the prince has insomnia) and Rebecca (I REFUSE to call her Bex) start bonding over the supernatural soap opera Devour (which I need to become a real thing in the worst way. My life is empty and meaningless without it), they gradually grow closer, until the weekend when Rebecca visits Windsor Castle where Nick has recreated her mother's Thanksgiving dinner exactly, so she won't feel so homesick, and they fall into each other's arms. Of course being the girlfriend to the heir to the throne, especially when you're an American to boot, isn't easy, and for years there is a lot of sneaking around in secret, until they are caught on camera by a paparazzi. Then things get even more difficult. 
 Since the book starts with Rebecca about to marry Nick, it's really not a surprise to the reader that although their romance is far from easy, and they even spend quite some time broken up, they are eventually going to get back together, and Rebecca will clearly be accepted by the Royal family - or there would be no wedding. I'm not sure if the authors intended the identity of the blackmailer to be a surprise, it seemed pretty obvious to me from fairly early on who it was going to be. 
 I read this book during the Spring Read-a-thon, and I suspect reading it over so many hours made me more a bit more frustrated with some sections of the book than if I'd read it over a few days. The extended section where Rebecca and Nick are broken up, and Rebecca goes on an extended bender got boring pretty fast and the complications that lead to Rebecca being blackmailed in the latter half of the book felt very forced to me. I'm not sure if that subplot was entirely necessary and it weakened the ending of the book for me. 
 Mostly, this was a highly entertaining romp, even more fun than the Fug Girls' YA books Spoiled and Messy. I must admit that their Royalty coverage is among the posts I skip during my weekly visits to the Go Fug Yourself website, because the older I get, the more convinced I am that monarchy should be abolished and that the royals are useless parasites draining an obscene amount of taxpayer money in the countries that they represent (including my own home country and that of my birth). I also had the dubious pleasure of going to St. Andrews university when Prince William enrolled there in my fourth year, so housing prices in town rose virtually overnight, due to the huge influx of rich Americans and Europeans enrolling at the Uni to get a glimpse of his highness. Now, a decade later, there are little signs up all over the place purporting to be coffee shops or pubs where the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge spent time. 
 While I think the monarchy is an outdated idea, it doesn't mean that I can't enjoy this book which is pretty much Will and Kate fan fiction. Playboy prince Freddie and the more and more preposterous names of his many girlfriends - a true delight, as are most of the supporting characters in Rebecca and Nick's circle of friends (my favourite may have ended up being Bea, Lady Bollocks herself). I suspect Rebecca is a more down to earth and grounded person than the woman she's modelled on (because while she may be a commoner, her father was one of the richest men in England even before his daughter married a prince) and from some of the stories I heard from friends and acquaintances, Nick in his student days kept a MUCH lower profile than William did. If you like celebrity gossip, pretty clothes, soapy intrigue, a modern fairy tale romance between a girl from Iowa and the heir to the British throne might be just what the doctor ordered. Personally, I'm going to try to figure out how to convince Heather Cocks and Jessica Morgan to pitch Devour to the CW so it can become a real thing. Vampires, witches, minotaurs, werewolves, shapeshifters, a private investigator who can smell the future, and panthers who seem like they know to much - how is this not on my TV already?

Before I Read the Book... 
 Part of me hoped this might be another companion book to If I Stay...Oh well. 
 Summary of the Story 
 Cody's best friend meg kills herself in the most organized way possible it's almost funny, but not really.  Cody is asked by Meg's parents to take a trip to Meg's apartment she lived in while going to school away from home. While there, she meets a boy who was involved with Meg. She notices Meg has a chunk of missing emails so she enlists the help of one of Meg's roommates to help find some files. They discover that Meg was contemplating suicide for a long time, and was part of a secret message board that encouraged it. One user in particular spoke to Meg so much that Cody is convinced he is to blame for Meg's death. She asks Meg's former fling Ben to drive her out to Nevada where she finds out the user lives, and she confronts him only to realize that Meg killed herself and she had to have wanted to with or without the man's help. She goes home, defeated, but not before sleeping with Ben and becoming even more devastated about the whole situation. Her mom puts her on a flight home, but Ben follows her and they reconcile, admitting they love each other and want to be together despite the less than ideal conditions under which they met in the first place. A year later they put Meg to rest by scattering her ashes, and Cody and Ben are still together, obviously.  
 While Reading 
 ** I already love Meg just for the fact that she begins her suicide note with "I regret to inform you". 
 ** Was she into Meg? Nah, I think I'm just reading too much into things. 
 ** It's like she joined a cult... 
 ** Yeah...hooking up with the guy your dead best friend liked probablyyyyyy isn't the most moral thing to do. 
 ** Yes, Cody. I'm so glad you figured out a century later to actually talk to the bullshit blog poster and get him to meet you or something. 
 ** I knew Tree seemed shady, more so than just your standard bitch. 
 ** LOL that BS guy fucked up hard by calling her. 
 ** Mehhhhhh it's still weird that she's with Ben.  
 What I Thought 
 I always find books post-suicide where characters have to piece together why that person chose to do it and how to move on without them interesting, no matter what. But interesting and good aren't necessarily the same thing. This book was good though -- not great -- but compared to other books I've read on the topic of suicide, this one does not rank among the best in my opinion. 
 I mean, an obvious reason for this is that Meg is kind of crazy for joining a suicide support group and basically looking up to a cult leader who encourages killing oneself while spouting quotation after quotation...I felt bad that Meg dealt with depression her whole life, but I couldn't get behind someone who was so naive to listen to someone online about taking their own life. Like, if you're going to do something like that, it should be no one's decision but your own.  
 Also, Cody annoyed the fuck out of me sometimes. I can't explain what exactly bothered me about her, but she got on my nerves sometimes. It also might have something to do with her losing her virginity to the guy her dead best friend lost her own virginity to (technically, since Meg's real first time was semi-rape). I don't know, that just seems fucked up. I know you like him, but....it's too weird.  
 I did like the story, but not enough to rave about it or think of recommending it to someone.

As PR said in the dedication - Married love is ever lasting love, and isn't that what we expect to find, as romance readers, when we pick up a romance novel? So...Why are books like this so rare? A unicorn, I tell you!!! 
 I have always loved books dealing with marriage and married couples. Maybe I'm wedding-crazy...

 But whatever the reason, I love them. without an exception. And... 
 I loved this one too. 
 I mean, come on. It's Penny Reid. I have yet to read a book by her that I haven't liked. She is genius when it comes to writing fresh and smart romantic comedies. Her characters are quirky and hilarious. They are flawed, weird and never fail to impress me with their encyclopedic knowledge. Knitting in the series maybe my favorite series of all time! 
 Okay so the story here is a bit different. We have Fiona (our heroine) who is an ex CIA agent but now stays at home with kids and is a super-soccer mom. Greg (our hero) wants to save the world, one oil- mine at a time. He travels all over the world on assignments and teaches people new ways to extract oil that's environmental friendly. Gah! In other words, he is a total average husband who wants things his way and then, charms his wife into giving in. A total dream...LOL! 
 But this time, his visit is different. Something has changed and Fiona isn't going to give in that easily. Hence, our adventure starts that takes us from Chicago to Nigeria and back. And yes, there's a ton of action in the middle, with the mundane problems of domestic life. 
 It kind of felt like Mr. and Mrs. Smith to me. 
 *Sigh* 
 All I gotta say is - if you're a fan of this series, you won't want to miss out on this installment. It's different with tons of action. But one thing remains the same - its hilarious and smart, PR's one of the best works. 
 And if you haven't read this series then...

Unlike most people, I can't marathon my series/trilogies and I usually read other books in between but that wasn't what happened with this trilogy. The writing, storyline, and characters were so addicting that I constantly needed more and when I had to put the book down, I was excited to pick it back up! It still is weird for me that the events of these books took place less than a month's time, but it felt much longer. I know a lot of people would be bothered by the insta-love between Gwen and Gideon, and I thought I would be too, but I really do think that so much has happened-with the traveling back and fourth in time-that it seemed like they had spent so much more time together than they actually had, so their love didn't really bother me at all. I adored all the past scenes between Gwen and Lucas, it was so adorable and I found those scenes to be some of my favorites. I still stand by the fact that Xemerius is my favorite character ever-I love all his little commentaries throughout the story, and how he was the comic relief throughout all the romantic scenes between Gideon and Gwen. The ending though...with Gwen being immortal unless she took her own life, was something that I didn't see coming. All those vague and mysterious verses about the 12, was confusing and I supposed I should have paid more attention to them but it did come as a surprise to me , oh and the traitor being Mr.Whitman! He always rubbed me the wrong way but I thought it was Mr.George because he seemed really nice...and I don't know I guess I was paranoid and Mr. George is simply just a nice person. , there's also the scene where Gideon gets shot but then it is revealed that he drank the salts and is now immortal! YAY! I was always worried about how they were going to be together and maybe it's cliche and all that, but I loved that they got their happy ending. , and lastly...when we find out that Gwen's butler or helper in the family is actually her nephew or something...aww! I thought it was so cute, that everyone in that house is truly family . This whole series just made me really happy and I found it to be such a good trilogy to read because it read like a television show, and I'm really sad that it's now over. The same reason I couldn't give this book a full five stars is because although I did really love it, it was missing something for me that I can't quite pinpoint but it was still an amazing read. I wish Kerstin Gier would continue the story though, I definitely would not protest to a few more books!

 "Shoot all the bluejays you want, if you can hit 'em, but remember it's a sin to kill a mockingbird." 
 A lawyer's advice to his children as he defends the real mockingbird of Harper Lee's classic novel- a black man charged with the rape of a white girl. 
 Reading this I went, 'Ok... Sounds like something heavy an advice.' It's meaning sets in only when you came towards the end of the book albeit you understand it's significance long before. 
 The story is narrated by a 6 year old girl, Jean-Louise Finch aka Scout. Scout, along with her brother Jem (Jeremy Atticus Finch) and their friend Dill (Charles Baker Harris), bring to us this tale. It is fascinating to see it through the eyes of children about the two strong issues in this book: Rape and Racial discrimination. Scout and Jem's father, Atticus Finch, a lawyer by profession, is the defender for a negro, Tom, who was been accused by a white family of rape. 
 The family lives in a small town, Maybcomb. It is described as a cosy, quiet place. The story begins with Jem and Scout meeting Dill. They become friends and as all little children, creatively indulge in their plays. Their summer days are described in the most innocent and beautiful manner. I couldn't help but smile at it all. Little things that kids do, and the meanings and reasons they put behind it- it's just fascinating! 
 The story steadily gets on to the serious topic of rape, where Scout asks, What is rape? She was 8 then. The trial as witnessed by the children is presented in the most emotional and energetic manner. The courtroom tension, anticipation all got to me. And when Dill started crying seeing how a white treats a colored man, saying, 'It's sick!, you see the simplicity of the situation naked. That a child having understood that there is no absolute reason in racial discrimination and yet there they were, all the adults, insulting the negros. 
 As Atticus says, 'They've done it before and they'll do it again and when they do it -- seems that only the children weep' 
 It isn't just the main plot of the story that is great. The lives of Jem and Scout, are so described that I saw my own childhood in there. The relationship shared between the brother and sister is very much like I share (or shared) with my own elder brother. However, I felt Jem and Scout were more lucky than I was, for having learned the lessons of life practically. Where they are supposed to read to their neighbor because they damaged her front garden... Where another neighbor of their's, Miss Maudie's house is on fire... The trial of course... Their little plays of Boo Radley and most of all their ability to reason out things with questions.  Another part which I hold close is of Scout being forced to be a 'lady' by her aunt. Being in my twenties, I face the same issue (even now yeah!). 
 Ladies in bunches always filled me with a vague apprehension and a firm desire to be elsewhere 
 To Kill a Mockingbird, is a rare book. It's 
 actually 
 one of it's kind! This book has given me back the wonderful memories of my childhood. It has reminded me of the way I saw life as a kid. As much as I love the life I lead now, it was a pleasure to get a peek of the past once. For the past directs the present and the future.
Love, love, LOVED it! Can't say I didn't see the end coming, but I loved it the whole way through!

This was a 3.75-4 star read for me. Why? Probably because I couldn't stand Lisa using Sol like she did. Trying to process my thoughts for a proper review. 
 Full review here: https://agingerlyreview.wordpress.com... 
 I was a little hesitant to read this after reading John Corey Whaley's book Noggin. That book was far too strange for me, plus it pissed me off. I didn't like how totally selfish the MC was. And in true me fashion, I thought all of his books might be like that so I stayed clear of them. I'm happy to say that this book was totally like that, only a little bit. 
 This is the story of Solomon and how he is agoraphobic with severe anxiety. He has a severe psychological break one day, ended up almost naked in the school fountain, and now hasn't stepped foot outside of his house in over three years. Sol is perfectly fine with his life now. Enter Lisa. Lisa wants to get into one of the best psychological colleges in the state and she plans on using Sol to help her get in. She is going to befriend Sol and "fix" him. She is going to write her admissions essay about Sol and BOOM get into college. What Lisa doesn't realize is that she, along with her boyfriend Clark, are going to form an instant and powerful friendship with Sol. All of them will be changed in ways they never dreamed possible. 
 This was a super fast read and it was a really interesting read. I was very curious to know how this story was going to play out. Sol was very comfortable staying home and never stepping foot outside. His parents were troubled by it, but they did not try to force him to do anything he didn't want to do. I appreciated that. Sol was a character that I would have liked to be friends with in real life. He had such a great sense of humor and knew what he liked. When Lisa came into his life, he was so excited that someone wanted to be his friend. Little did he know that Lisa was a big fat fake. I could feel my heart breaking for Sol as the story went on and he found out just what Lisa was all about. As you can tell from my Goodreads updates, I never liked Lisa from the beginning. 
 I don't usually trust someone - real or book character - that plans to use someone else for their own personal gain. That is exactly what Lisa was doing and I didn't care for it. She was going to use an innocent teenager who had serious psychological issues to help her get into to college and out of that small town. That's wrong on so many levels. A lot of people would say she was just being ambitious, driven, and possibly an over achiever. Me? I call her selfish and manipulative. 
 I also did not like how Lisa brought Clark, her boyfriend, into the friendship in order to help Sol get better faster. She was trying too hard to get Sol "fixed" and outside of the house that she used her boyfriend. I don't see how she thought pushing so much on Sol at once would make things better. Sol still had not set a single foot outside but Lisa thought bringing someone new over to engage in awkward conversation with Sol was a good idea? Especially after Sol confessed that he was gay? I'm a little lost here. None of that realistically makes sense to me. I also did not like how she was constantly trying to have sex with Clark. When I say constantly, I do mean all of the time. She was always making passes and advances at him. She was making me uncomfortable. Why was she in such a rush to sleep with him? And while she is in high school no less! Calm down your whoremones. 
 If you remove Lisa from the entire equation, I really enjoyed this story. I haven't read a story about a MC that is agoraphobic who had severe anxiety. I do wish the story had gone a little more into detail as to why he became one, but that didn't happen. I was left slightly confused on that front. I loved Sol as a character. He was heartwarming, charming, so funny, and an all around good soul. His family was great as well. I loved how supportive they were of Sol no matter what. That was refreshing to read. I also enjoyed Clark as a character. He did not complicate things since he was the one person that seemed to really want to be Sol's friend. Yes, Sol did fall in love with him but that might have been because Clark was the first teenage male he befriended in three years. I cannot fault Sol for that. 
 Overall, I would recommend this book to everyone. I think it is a raw and powerful read. I think it gives great insight into what it has to be like for an agoraphobic with anxiety. It is a great coming of age story. It is also a story of learning to accept yourself and come to terms with who you are. You do you and let everyone else do them. I hope everyone gives this book a chance. I hope everyone will come to adore Sol the way that I do.

I watched the show without knowing that it's actually an adaption from a book. Naturally, being an avid reader that I am, I waste no time in searching for the book to read it. Despite being a great show, the book somehow is lacking in a lot of areas. It is uncommon for a movie/tv show to be better than the books but it has happened and in this case, it happened again. 
 First and foremost, as unusual as it is, the tv show has more character development and depth compared with the book. *gasp* This is highly disappointing as you'd expect that to be the opposite. Also, as absurd as it sounds, the author had not made an effort to describe her characters (or I may have missed it?) aside from a select few like Clarke who from all that I've read had gathered that she has "shiny blonde hair that shines from the sunlight/moonlight" or Octavia that was mentioned as being chubby and has wide blue eyes. This is quite maddening because this is a novel and descriptions of the characters' features are as essential as the plots itself. If it weren't for the show, I will have no idea what's going on in the story and I will have fits from reading the book! It seems like the tv show completes the book and fills in the missing plots and added in characters that's essential to the show. 
 Somehow, the book felt incomplete in the sense that we weren't told in depth what happened to earth and how exactly were the people in The Ark was sent to space. It would have been better if the book had mentioned and elaborate more in that areas. So we were introduced to a post-apocalyptic world where humans live in space in some sort of a space station called The Ark. We weren't told how they survived in the space station or how exactly they got there in the first place. The settings were bland and nonconstructive in the sense that it is not majorly involve in the story but only serves as an essential background for the story. 
 It became clear after a few chapters that this book is not so much about surviving in a post-apocalyptic world as it is about romance. From early on we were introduced to Wells Jaha (the son of the Chancellor) who committed a crime that had the potential to endanger the lives of everyone on board The Ark just so he can be with his "one true love" (selfish much?). Not that the Chancellor had any problem in sending his only son to an uncertain fate at the earth that could highly potentially kill his son. Despite what Wells had done to be with Clarke (his one true "love"), Clarke was not any more appreciative of him 
 than she is with anything else. I can understand that Clarke resented Wells because he did "something" that betrayed her but what I hate about her is that she is so uncertain in making her choice. At first she hate Wells then she make up with him because he saved her from an almost sure death (*rolls eyes*). Ironically, she broke up with him again after that because he was trying to stop her from another certain death by running into the fire to save someone. Guess what she did next? She ran away with another guy. 
 Thus, ensues a love triangle war! (In the second book I guess.) 
 All in all, The 100 is a bland and boring story that centers mostly around young romance and completely lack of the post-apocalyptic world that I was expecting. I love the show though. It is million times better than the book. I will continue watching the show but I can't say the same for the book.

What a delightful story! One thing I love about steampunk is how creative the authors are. Just the concept alone, of clockwork children secretly replacing human children is fantastic. Add in hags and ogres and swamps and dragons, not to mention mechanical maids, spyder spies on the walls, woodland dwellers, and a plot to overthrow the kingdom, and I found this story fully entertaining. 
 The writing has come such a long way from the other book I read by Jordan Elizabeth (Escape from Witchwood Hollow), and the construction of the plot much more in depth and complete. Her skill has definitely grown. There were places that still felt a little stilted to me, and I can't quite put my finger on it. Things jumped around a little bit too much, too. I could understand at the end when the main event was going down, but at times things felt a little jumbled. Otherwise, I can't say I found much wrong with this one. 
 With no profanity or sex, this story rates as family friendly to me. It does get a bit dark with some fairly graphic violence at the end, but it is brief. 
 A solid 4 stars - it will be 5 on Amazon.

Harry Blackstone Copperfield Dresden 
 A wizard and an all around a nice kind of guy. 
 I had no idea I would enjoy this book as much as I did. Butcher created an amazing character and his writing style is smooth and seamless. This book flows from one page to the next. 
 What really impressed me with Harry Dresden is just how much of an ordinary guy he really is, and just how much a badass he managed to be. There was no stupid posturing, cheesy one liners or testosterone driven Neanderthalism. He even made a back duster seem cool. And considering how far back this book was written just how many cliches involving a black duster there are, that is a feat and a half. 
 There are not many urban fantasy series out there that take their time in a way like Jim Butcher writes, there are even less involving male main characters. The plot stretches out like a warm summer's night and you still manage to stop and smell the roses on your way to the finish line. Not a single part of it seemed rushed and all the supporting characters had a lived in feel, like they've truly lived all their lives right where they were supposed to be, and we are just simply passing by at the moment being nosey. Although this is only my first book by Jim Butcher, I already know that this is a classic series, a 'don't miss'. And I don't intend to. 
 It's also quite refreshing to have a guy's perspective when it comes to flirting and romance. Dresden embodies a genuinely nice guy with the odds stacked against him when it comes to women. Although by his train of thought you can clearly see that he is a full blooded male, his actions speak of his insecurities and loneliness. Not many guys out there that write like this. It's like there is some bro code that requires male characters to be limited to a certain pre written book of conduct around women. The end result is always uninspired. 
 Bob the skull though.... He is the best supporting character I have met in the last couple years for sure. A wiseass, horndog spirit trapped in a skul whose soul purpose (soul purpose hihihi) was to accumulate information because Wizards and tech don't mix.

MINI-REVIEW: 
 "Eyes of Silver, Eyes of Gold" is a beautiful love story of a man and a woman united together against the world. 
 Anne and Cord's marriage is born from a violent encounter not of their doing, and their love slowly unfolds through their first year of marriage as they deal with the struggles of prejudice, her family's hatred, his family's mistrust and Cord's inability to open up emotionally. 
 While the romance is wonderful, the writing needs a deft editor's hand. Events are summarized and retold, details skipped to be told at a later point. My frustration with the writing battled with my admiration for the love story. This tale is an unpolished diamond, reminding me of Dana Ransom's old western romances. 
 All in all, I am glad I read this book and hope the author finds an understanding editor to help polish her future works into flawless gems.

 My thoughts: Inio Asano is a very acclaimed author in the manga world, so he was in my radar for a long time. I read Nijigahara Holograph by him earlier this year and enjoyed it to some extent. I had my issues with it, but all in all, it was a solid horror manga. 
 I went into Solanin expecting the same amount of criticism of human morale and human selfishness and I sort of did get what I expected, but also sort of didn't. Solanin is very different than Nijigahara Holograph. 
 First, I would characterize this book as a slice of life story. The main characters', Mieko and Naruo, 'quarter-life crisis' was in focus here, as well as their relation to the world they inhabit. Nothing is going the way Meiko and Naruo had dreamed of in their college days. The days are the same, and the characters keep going 'round and 'round in a non-stop cycle of work and responsibilities (or their futile trials of escape from responsibilities). Until, that is, Mieko gets a revelation and decides to quit her job, thus spiraling her and Naruo's life towards a risky, but more exciting future. Things go wrong, though, because they are the people they are and the society is the same society - both things are inescapable. 
 I like the story's perspective on this 'quarter-life crisis' and I feel with the characters, which are on the threshold from childhood (or perhaps, innocence is a better word) towards adulthood. No one prepares you for what adulthood is, and you must find your own footing once you step over this threshold. The way the story was told and presented, though, was a tad heavy-handed. Some events in the story don't make a whole lot of sense, and don't get me started on the conclusions the characters draw throughout the book! There's no rhyme or reason to many of the characters' decisions - maybe it was the author's intention, but if that's the case, it isn't done very well. Overall, it was an OK book, but I expected more. 
 Verdict: 3/5 stars. Read it if you like the synopsis - the book is good, but nothing that hasn't been done before.

Nothing makes me skeptical like the words "next Harry Potter." Usually it has less to do with charm or quality, and more to do with financial expectations. 
 So it was with caution that I approached "The Bone Season," the first book in a new urban sci-fantasy series by young author Samantha Shannon. And after reading it, I can assure the world -- this is not Harry Potter. Instead, it's an interesting but clumsily-handled story that needs a bit more editing to make it work. 
 It takes place in a dystopian Britain at the end of the 21st century. People with psychic powers (aka "voyants") have been outlawed by the evil government, forcing them to work secretly in criminal syndicates who compete against each other. Teenage Paige Mahoney (aka "The Pale Dreamer") is a dreamwalker, which is a rare type of clairvoyant. 
 And after a disastrous incident on a train, Paige ends up captured and dragged to Oxford, which is now controlled by the Rephaim, a mysterious, powerful race who want to use all voyants. Given to Warden Arcturus, the Rephaim want to use her talents for their own ends -- but Paige is determined to regain her freedom at all costs. 
 "The Bone Season" is very visibly a first novel. Samantha Shannon has an intriguing, mold-breaking idea for a world, with lots of psychics, mysterious other races, technology that can "read auras" and a seamless blend of fantasy and sci-fi. It's a complicated world, and she has a lot of intriguing ideas that she weaves into a plot that I haven't seen before. 
 The problem is the execution, which is rather clumsy. Shannon also seems to have taken "show, don't tell" to heart -- she shows us everything, but tells us little. Characters are plunked down as if we should know who they are, and she often doesn't explain what is going on. Showing is good, but a little telling is necessary to not confuse the audience. 
 She also has a somewhat mixed writing style. It's vivid and atmospheric, with powerful descriptions of everything that Paige experiences and feels -- and psychic powers are a difficult thing to pull off. However, her prose needs to be smoothed out. She uses words too long and complicated for the scenes she inserts them into ("Nuala had a permeable dreamscape") which just reminds you that you're reading a book. It's hard to lose yourself in it. 
 Paige is an interesting heroine as well -- she's strong but sometimes bratty, prickly but scrappy. She's got a lot of guts, and it's nice to see that kind of protagonist reentering the literary world after years of Bella Swans. 
 Samantha Shannon obviously has bright ideas and raw talent, but "The Bone Season" needed a bit more refinement before it sprang out into the world. All the same, keep an eye out for Paige's next adventure.

As I wrote this review, I became increasingly pissed off. I just finished writing it and damn it all to hell, I want to shred something to smithereens. 
 Do you know how many chances I gave this series? Five. 
 Five. 
 That's more chances than I've ever given to anything. 
 The first time I picked up this book was when I was 13. I was a hormonal mess at that age, as we all were. I loved any and every YA book I got my hands on. And I powered through the series somehow (by what sorcery, I don't bloody know). I think I made it halfway through Dark Flame. Hell, I don't know how I managed that. 
 Second time I picked it up was after I abandoned reading for school. I remembered I loved this series (for the love of sanity, wtf was wrong with me?!) but I had forgotten what happened in the novels so I started from book one. I think I finished it. 
 Third time was when I abandoned reading again for my studies. I picked up Evermore from the library because, again, I'd forgotten what happened. Didn't finish it. 
 Fourth time I picked it up was because I hated leaving a series unfinished. Grabbed it from the library and loathed every minute of it so I stopped before reaching half of it. 
 Years later, I read it for the fifth time. And I forced myself to finish it. I freaking hated it. My god, did I hate it. 
 Who says "I mean" that bloody often? The more or less chaste, undying, tulip love was cute at first, and then it wasn't. It wasn't love; it was like making a robot walk as naturally as a human. It felt forced, wrong, and just 
 no. 
 I detested Ever. I'm not explaining this. I'd end up crushing the keys of my keyboard if I did. 
 Screw Damen. He loves Ever to eternity's end but where is the substance of love? Where is the honesty, the respect, the learning, the compromising? What. The. Hell. 
 This whole story was a waste of my teenage years. SIDUGHSDUKHFKH for crying out loud, this was horrible. 
 I gave it a one star for the sole reason of honouring my attempts. Five chances, ya'll. Friggin' five. 
 Now, excuse me as I try to hold in my seething irritation. Goodness, this book pissed me off.
I liked it, but I hated both of the guys that Sarina lusted after. She could have done better, and if she were a real person that I knew, I'd tell her that.

I am tired of this series. I need a break. Yes, it was a good story and yes, it wasn't EXACTLY like the previous two books. Her spending habits take a backstage to her wedding debacle. But....Yes, there is a but. It really is the same story rehashed with different players and an altered focus on the story line. We still see Becky make the wrong decisions. For every step forward that she makes in a previous book, she takes a mile back in the next. It is almost like she starts over with zero progression. It was worse between the first and the second book. I don't think between the 2nd and the 3rd is as bad. It's like the author is cashing in on writing the same story over again. That's why I think that I need to take a break from the series. I'm not enjoying it as much anymore. I need to revisit it at a later time and see if I still feel the same about it. If you have loved the previous two books, then you will love this one, because you won't understand where I'm coming from. Don't let my review stop you from reading it. If you agree the same with me, then you understand my frustration with the author. I love the characters. I just want to see Becky grow and continue to grow instead of always taking a step back. She needs a new adventure w/o the problems of her being very materialistic. What about a baby problem? Or something along those lines. I need something new in the next book to keep me reading, but for now, I'm not reading the next one for quite some time. Maybe next year.

 Carter was also wonderful. This boy was so sweet and I totally adored him. He was very charming and he sure knew how to woo a girl. I thought he was perfect. 
 The romance was lovely. Penelope and Carter were great together. They were perfectly matched in their personality and their power. And the chemistry between them was there from the moment they met. I thought they were great together. 
 The plot was good. I was kept interested, but I wasn't totally hooked. And, I would have liked to have seen more explanation about all the magic. There were a few times when I was a bit lost. But, I still enjoyed the story and the ending has me curious to see what happens next. 
 Salt was a wonderful YA paranormal romance. I really enjoyed reading this fantastic book. YA romance lovers, this is a book worth checking out.
